title: Airport Chaos Began Long Before the Ground Stop
excerpt: Every civilian airplane in the United States has been told not to fly, owing to a nationwide FAA ground stop
body: Every civilian airplane in the United States has been told not to fly, owing to a nationwide FAA ground stop
As I write this, very little is known about the nature of the safety risk or the issue underlying it
According to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, “a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers” necessitated the action, which was undertaken for reasons of safety
The stop could keep planes on the ground for hours, or much longer
Even when the stop ends, unwinding the inevitable backup will take more time
If you’re in the air, your plane will land
But if you are at the airport waiting for one, it might be best to give up and go home
In a sense, chaos such as this arrived long before today
Air travel has become terrible, and it has done so slowly and over a long period of time
In terms of safety, air travel is far less dangerous than driving, although an erosion of oversight, funding, infrastructure, and other factors might be changing that
James Fallows, a longtime contributor to The Atlantic , just wrote a lengthy article for The New York Times Magazine about exactly this risk
Setting aside actual safety, the experience of traveling by commercial airline has been getting worse and worse for years
Once blue with clarity, the American skies are now clouded with uncertainty
My son’s flight from Boston to LaGuardia was delayed earlier today, before the ground stop, by weather. “You should have taken the train,” I texted him
He made it out mere hours before all planes were grounded
New York City–area airports have suffered delays in recent days due to weather—a seemingly constant issue flying in or out of that city
My son and his sister, who both live in Manhattan, decided months ago not to even try to leave town for Thanksgiving, because delays and cancellations have become so commonplace
Industry consolidation reduced routes to medium-size cities, sending more passengers through a smaller number of hubs
Passengers might have to make connections for routes that once flew direct, or drive longer distances to reach a bigger airport
Extreme weather has worsened flying conditions headed into and out of almost any airport, making arrivals and departures less reliable
Delays and disruptions can mean that equipment and crews don’t arrive for a flight on time or at all
Even when the planes and pilots are available, the Air Route Traffic Control Centers are more sparsely staffed than they once were, while the number of flights each one manages has increased
The ARTCCs are FAA facilities distributed around the country, each one responsible for guiding aircraft through a specific region’s airspace
For example, the Chicago center handles northern Illinois and parts of Wisconsin, Iowa, Indiana, and Michigan
That center might hand off traffic bound for Dallas to the Kansas City center, or to Indianapolis for planes en route to Atlanta

What airport-control towers do for takeoff and landing, these centers do for the cruising portion of a flight—keeping aircraft safely spaced out from one another by assigning them altitudes or by guiding pilots around weather

On the internet, where citizens seem to revel in conspiracism, some people have connected today’s FAA ground stop with yesterday’s Microsoft Outlook outage —and the murky notion that advanced AI models might be responsible for both, and more
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at a news conference that a cyberattack is unlikely to have caused ground stop
Even so, a Government Accountability Office report from September identified threats in certain aspects of FAA communication systems that malicious actors could, in principle, exploit
And just yesterday, the FAA expanded the use of an AI-based air-traffic-management tool to all 22 control centers

The controllers on the ground may not know much about the cause yet, either. “We lost all of our approach frequencies, and other facilities did too,” an air-traffic controller based in the Midwest told The Atlantic . “For this to be affecting multiple facilities nationwide doesn’t make any sort of sense.” Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport has run out of tarmac space already, causing planes to be diverted elsewhere, the controller added. “This is going to be a mess for days, if not weeks.” Whatever the cause, once the delays inevitably happen, even big, newer airports often become inhospitable hosts
Long walks through huge hubs now feel required
Limited seating at gates makes waits of any kind uncomfortable

Frequent flyers don’t fare much better, because long queues to get into overcrowded lounges have turned those spots into marginally less horrible waiting rooms (albeit ones that also offer free cheese)

The frequent traveling that would formerly have gotten you into those lounges (or upgraded to first class after leaving them, should your flight actually depart) has become optional; the airlines have found that travelers are willing to pay for those perks instead, or earn them by spending money with their airline-branded credit cards

Customer service can be truculent or impossible, requiring long telephone wait times, confusing and unreliable apps, or the traversal of even more airport hallways to self-service kiosks—none of which are guaranteed to produce results
The entire experience of flying is adversarial

When travelers do get disrupted, like so many have been today and will be this weekend (and perhaps subsequently), they are likely to get limited assistance from the airlines, which now have more limited incentives to help and reduced consequences for failing to do so
This ground stop is not the airlines’ fault, but travelers have become inured to being treated badly no matter the cause of their travel headaches

Almost exactly a year ago, the Department of Transportation withdrew initiatives that the Biden administration had put in place to require compensation, meals, lodging, and rebooking for airline-caused disruptions, such as equipment failures

Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November
A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm (13.97in) in 12 hours
In Lisbon, 183 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, about a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations
After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy
This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera
The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia

Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas

title: Vance’s Gamble Looks Shakier Now
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Vance was a wealthy man and a best-selling author, but he wanted more
With Trump’s backing, Vance wagered, he might become president
For a while, that looked like a good bet: Trump helped Vance overcome an underwhelming campaign to become a senator from Ohio, then chose him as a running mate in 2024
Trump treated him as his heir apparent, and Vance’s most obvious rival, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, said he wouldn’t run in 2028 if the veep did
In a 60 Minutes interview this weekend, Trump said he might not endorse anyone in the coming GOP primary. “I may or may not get involved,” he said . “I don’t know

Maybe I’m better off not getting involved.” No one, not even Trump, can say whether he’ll really stay out of it, but he famously enjoys pitting his aides and employees against one another , which a withheld endorsement might achieve
Besides, Trump is at a political low after the midterms, and forcing would-be successors to compete for his favor is one way he can still exert control

Would his endorsement be much of a prize for Vance, or anyone else? This is the bind that any aspiring Republican presidential candidate will confront ahead of 2028: They need Trump’s support, or at least can’t afford his animosity, because even in his weakened state, his base remains loyal and potentially decisive in a primary
But as the GOP’s disastrous results this month show, being seen as too close to Trump can also be a major liability
You can watch Vance attempting to navigate this trap in recent days
In a lengthy postelection analysis on X, the vice president—a reported skeptic of the war in Iran—pinned the blame for poor Republican performance on the war

This had the advantage of distracting from all the other unpopular parts of the MAGA platform that Vance does support, but it also looks a lot like either a criticism of Trump or an attempt to nudge him into an anti-war position—risky either way

Yesterday, Trump announced that he was pulling Vance off his duty of negotiating with Iran, assigning him instead “to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.” (How this is different from Vance’s previous detail as “fraud czar” is not totally clear—though given Democratic gains at the state level this month, the remit has certainly widened.) Trump added that “we don’t need a deal with Iran
Those days have long since passed.” The new assignment is a Rorschach test

Is it a punishment for Vance for getting out of line on Iran? (The vice president was also reportedly considering new direct talks with Iran when Trump made the change.) Is Trump giving Vance a thankless, amorphous task that will further alienate domestic audiences who have already turned against the White House? Or is Trump helping Vance by pulling him off a dead-end role and allowing him to create some distance from the Iran debacle? (Trump could also just be acting impulsively.) Vice presidents tend to get stuck with these types of vague, impossible tasks, which later become electoral baggage
It was one of Kamala Harris’s big challenges in 2024

But Vance and Harris share a larger disadvantage. “There basically isn’t any good example since presidential approval ratings began of the VP to an unpopular president later being elected president himself,” Nate Silver notes

Maybe that’s one reason, according to a CNN report today , “Vance has given serious consideration to not running for president in 2028 after last week’s calamitous midterm elections.” The article cites conversations with “roughly a dozen allies and advisers.” Yet The Washington Post also reports today that Vance is “still more likely to run for president than not,” a conclusion based on conversations with—you guessed it—“more than a dozen people with a view into the vice president’s orbit.” Although Vance has consistently led 2028-primary polls at this early stage, a Reuters/Ipsos poll this week found Rubio slightly ahead of him

One poll is just one poll, and I’ve written that Rubio will have the same can’t-win-with-Trump, can’t-win-without-him dynamic that Vance does, especially because he’s the secretary of state and national security adviser during the Iran war. (There’s also the matter of him using taxpayer money to fly military jets to watch his son’s football team, as my colleague Sally Jenkins writes today.) But the result does suggest Vance’s vulnerability
With the nomination looking more available, other Republicans are also suddenly making themselves visible
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis offered some sharp statements about the direction of the GOP after the midterms, evidently positioning himself as an alternative
But the 2024 Republican primary showed DeSantis’s limits as a campaigner—and the difficulty he faced in trying to be both an inheritor and alternative to Trumpism

Former Vice President Pence is interested too ; a Pence campaign would test whether a Republican can win with the rare combination of being both tainted by association with Trump and also detested by him
Louisiana Senator John Kennedy apparently wants to see whether a candidate can succeed on the basis of folksy aphorisms delivered in an exaggerated drawl
On Kalshi, the prediction market, traders still see Vance as the most likely nominee , but they have John McEntee as fourth

McEntee is no household name; he was a personal aide to Trump in his first term but was pushed out over alleged problem gambling, and since then has become a TikTok influencer and the founder of a right-wing dating site
Whether McEntee’s place in the market is more an indictment of Kalshi’s usefulness or the 2028 Republican presidential bench is difficult to say

title: I’ve Been With Trump Since 2016. Hegseth Should Resign.
excerpt: “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.” The loud rebuke of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his entourage by an Army s
body: “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.” The loud rebuke of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his entourage by an Army sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day was the latest embarrassment of the defense chief’s tenure
For nearly two years, Hegseth has treated the Pentagon as a backdrop for self-promotion
He would serve President Trump best by stepping down before Democrats use him to help jam up the president’s agenda during Trump’s final two years in office
I first worked for Trump on his 2016 campaign in Trump Tower
I served in his White House as a deputy assistant to the president and chief spokesperson for the National Security Council
In Trump’s second term, I volunteered to help Hegseth stand up his press office by serving him for a short time as a senior adviser and spokesperson
Twenty years ago, I was spokesperson for the Senate Armed Services Committee when another defense secretary became the face of an unpopular war and a millstone around the neck of President George W
As I write in my new memoir of my years working for Trump, loyalty in his second term has usually been measured by how loudly an appointee defends him
But real loyalty means sometimes telling the president what he does not want to hear, including about yourself
An appointee whose missteps are hurting the president needs to think hard about whether he has become a political liability and offer to step aside when that’s the case
That duty begins before an appointee accepts the job
If the president offered me the post of deputy attorney general, the loyal answer would be, “Thank you, Mr

But you might want someone with a law degree.” Hegseth, a former Fox News weekend co-host and major in the Minnesota National Guard who had never run a large organization, should have known that he was not qualified to lead the largest department in the federal government
He was confirmed 51 to 50 , with the vice president breaking the tie
A nominee who squeaks in on that margin has every reason to lower the volume
He turned it up instead. [ Tom Nichols: Pete Hegseth lashes out ] On January 3, Democrats will take firm control of the House
The 211–204 vote to shelve an impeachment resolution this week, with 11 Democrats not present, was a reprieve for Hegseth, not a vindication

Whether or not Democrats impeach him next year, they will have the gavels and the subpoena power, and every hearing on Hegseth will be a week the White House spends doing something other than advancing its agenda
Hegseth is the least qualified defense secretary in modern memory
Voters have noticed: 32 percent approve and 57 percent disapprove of his performance, according to a Quinnipiac poll from September

He has been the Cabinet’s most visible champion of a war in Iran that has cost more than a dozen American lives, closed the Strait of Hormuz, and burned through nearly 80 percent of our THAAD (Terminal High Altitude Area Defense) interceptors
He has turned the military into a stage in the culture wars

At Marine Corps Base Quantico in September, before an audience the Pentagon had screened based on waist-to-height standards , he said : “No fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals
Just warriors.” He added, “The ideological clowns are out
The patriotic cowboys are in, with testosterone testing on top.” He films workouts with troops and posts them to official accounts

He planned to livestream the firing-squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter until Trump called off the macabre spectacle. [ Read: Democrats are ready to run Hegseth ‘out of town’ ] He has pushed out top military leaders and two of the three service secretaries the president appointed, Dan Driscoll and John Phelan
Two of his closest advisers were marched out of the Pentagon over leak accusations that went nowhere
He undermined the chain of command by intervening in at least two investigations into dangerous low-altitude flights

He shared prestrike details of a U.S. operation in Yemen over Signal with his wife, his brother, and his lawyer, which the Pentagon’s inspector general found had risked “ potential harm to U.S. pilots .” In September 2025, a follow-up, or “double tap,” strike on an alleged drug boat in the Caribbean killed two survivors clinging to the wreckage, after which The Washington Post reported that Hegseth had given a verbal order to “kill everybody.” He denies making the order, but lawmakers in both parties have warned that it could be a war crime
Each of these is a hearing waiting to happen
In 2006, Republicans lost both the House and the Senate in a midterm dominated by another unpopular war in the Middle East
Then–Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld read the political mood and stepped down rather than weaken his boss and his party by hanging on
Bush replaced him with Robert Gates, whose low-key professionalism steadied the Pentagon
Rumsfeld’s departure was an act of loyalty
This week, at his first press conference in six months, he shouted scripted bromides into the cameras for his customary audience of one, arguing that he should keep his job
When a defense secretary has to make a public case that he is not an embarrassment to the president, he has already lost the battle
Hegseth awarded a medal to the sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier after a public backlash
But it should not take a soldier to remind a secretary of defense about the decorum his office demands
The president deserves better, as do the members of our military.

title: Rebuilding a World That Never Existed
excerpt: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
body: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
When it comes to reading, I’m not a glutton for punishment—I didn’t get very far into Finnegans Wake —but I am drawn to interesting challenges
Among the most memorably difficult reads I’ve taken on was the 1926 book A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle

A cerebral but darkly funny epic poem whose plot is well summarized by its title, it is written in “synthetic Scots,” a language cobbled together from Scottish dialects by its author, Hugh MacDiarmid. (Although Scots survives as a minority language with many regional variations, none of them closely resemble MacDiarmid’s concoction.) I loved the verse for its woozy lyricism and nerded out on the text’s annotations; I was also fascinated by the author’s grand ambitions
MacDiarmid was part of a cultural movement known as the Scottish Renaissance, whose writers sought to revive the once-independent nation’s dialects and traditions

But did he really think he could kick off a national resurgence by inventing a language no reader could easily understand? And what would drive a writer to even try? This week, the Atlantic staff writer Lily Meyer explored a similar question in her article about What Remains , a novel written by Brais Lamela in Galician

First, here are six new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: The one source Bob Woodward can’t get to talk How to be an ethical Russophile The worst thing about AI writing “Memories of the Train,” a short story by Siqi Liu AI is destroying the trust between writers and readers. “Poem for the WaterShed,” a poem by Gretel Ehrlich Meyer calls Lamela’s choice to write in a language primarily spoken in a single region in the northwest of Spain “an artistic expression of commitment to his particular roots,” and it is—but Lamela also understands the futility of trying to re-create the past

The novel’s narrator is writing a thesis about a widow in Galicia, who resisted the dictator Francisco Franco’s effort to subjugate the area (the government flooded rural villages and banned the Galician language)
Yet the narrator’s academic ambitions are as nostalgic as they are political

Feeling rootless and isolated in New York, he hopes, Meyer writes, “to create a home of some sort for the unsettled parts of himself.” Other authors in minority languages have been vocal about their motivations

Writers in Greenlandic, Basque, Welsh, and the Judeo-Spanish language of Ladino have eschewed dominant languages such as Spanish or English to preserve cultures that have been subsumed by larger nations

Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o forsook English to write in Kikuyu, publicly rebelling against England’s rule in Kenya and explaining that he wanted to “reconnect to the patriotic traditions” of a “literature rooted among the people.” MacDiarmid, too, saw himself as resisting the English and their language; he hated them so much that he once wrote, in private correspondence, that he might prefer a Nazi victory over England
But unlike Ngũgĩ, who wrote in a language spoken by millions, the Scot was trying to build a lexicon that had never really existed

In this sense he is not unlike Lamela’s narrator, a person who finds “re-creation” to be, Meyer writes, “a source of stability as much as it is an escape.” Characters like this, Meyer adds, “aspire to inhabit history so fully that they might create a home, or at least a moment of rest and acknowledgment, for its unsettled ghosts.” Such attempts might be doomed to fail, but that doesn’t mean they aren’t noble, or even beautiful
MacDiarmid didn’t exactly rebuild Scottish literature, but he made a modernist work of art that I’ll never forget

Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic A Novel About Obsessively Digging Into the Past By Lily Meyer A new book by the Galician writer Brais Lamela chronicles the drive that many have to touch history, no matter how elusive it is

What to Read Dirtbag, Massachusetts , by Isaac Fitzgerald Though his memoir-in-essays is subtitled A Confessional , and though it opens by revising the story he and his family used to tell about his childhood, Fitzgerald doesn’t immediately lay bare the lingering pain of his tumultuous upbringing

The first 11 essays are plenty vulnerable: Fitzgerald writes that he was born of an affair; spent his early years living in a homeless shelter and then in low-income housing run by the Catholic Worker movement; moved to north-central Massachusetts, where “violence was the solution, problem, and consequence”; and began abusing alcohol and drugs before age 13
But these are mere “flashes of the past,” as Fitzgerald writes in the last essay, “My Story,” where he takes full control of the narrative of his life

As he admits to having avoided the full truth, Fitzgerald becomes his own confessor, the one with the power to forgive. — Kristen Martin From our list: Six books you should read twice Out Next Week 📚 On the Calculation of Volume (Book V) , by Solvej Balle 📚 The Imperfect City , by Paul Goldberger 📚 Love the Revolution , by Aleksandr I

Solzhenitsyn Your Weekend Read Illustration by Tina Zhou / The Atlantic Zelda ’s Midlife Crisis By Ian Bogost This idea, that a video game could facilitate exploration in a simulated world bigger than the challenges choreographed inside it, is now so familiar that it counts as cliché
Popular culture—even Star Wars —was not yet understood by its consumers as world building, a now-popular name for constructing a fictional universe and then situating characters and stories inside it
Tolkien had been popular for decades, of course, but high fantasy was still largely considered escapist and—apologies—somewhat cringeworthy
To obsess about a false world real enough to imagine occupying remained strange, a fixation of dweebs unable or unwilling to live in the real one

title: Silicon Valley’s Chaos Moment
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube As the Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has fallen this week—shaking the American economy, which AI helps hold togethe
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube As the Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has fallen this week—shaking the American economy, which AI helps hold together—Anthropic prepares for an IPO at an expected valuation of up to $1.4 trillion
In this episode, Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel talks about Huang’s resignation, and the danger of having such a figure bear the weight of the economy
Then he talks to the Vox reporter Sigal Samuel about Anthropic’s IPO, how the AI race has influenced the company’s ideology, and why it and other companies refuse to slow down or stop
The following is a transcript of the episode: Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain
We’ve got a great episode for you today where we talk to Vox reporter Sigal Samuel about the AI race and Anthropic’s upcoming IPO
But first, there is very big news that I need to address
On Thursday morning, Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia and arguably the most important figure in the world of artificial intelligence, resigned from the company
This is a shocking development that just one week ago seemed utterly impossible
Huang’s resignation came after reports that he was engaged in an extramarital affair with a businesswoman who, turns out, was an asset for Chinese intelligence
Huang admitted to the relationship, Silicon Valley circled the wagons to defend him, while many in Congress demanded investigations into Huang, Nvidia, and its relationship to China
And the logic for keeping him in place was very simple

Huang is seen as the visionary of the AI boom—a man who, more than a decade before generative AI, made this bet that his graphics-processor company could be used to train neural networks and artificial intelligence
It was an unpopular decision, but Huang held course
He was patient, and over time the bet paid off
Nvidia became the company that built the chips that would train and help power AI data centers and models

As The New Yorker ’s Stephen Witt wrote in a 2023 profile of Huang , “The revelation that ChatGPT … had been trained on an Nvidia supercomputer spurred one of the largest single-day gains in stock-market history.” And Nvidia became this juggernaut: one of the most valuable companies of all time
Just last month, Nvidia’s valuation hit $5.7 trillion, which is larger than every economy except the United States and China
And some estimates suggest that Nvidia provided 90 percent of the advanced chips used in the AI industry
And Huang used Nvidia’s endless profits to become arguably the lead investor in the artificial-intelligence boom
He famously saw the industry as this five-layer cake of components, and he pledged to distribute Nvidia’s money and technology across every layer of it
The company, as of July, had invested $99 billion into AI companies—including OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX, and data-center providers like CoreWeave
He pioneered this circular style of investment, where companies pay Nvidia for the chips, and then Nvidia puts that money back into the companies, in part so they can keep buying chips
Now, some saw this as genius, right? The Bank of Nvidia
And others saw this as the beginnings of what could turn into a disastrous bubble
But regardless, Huang—who brokered many of these deals himself—and Nvidia, they both affixed themselves as this load-bearing beam of the AI boom
And Nvidia’s success wasn’t just guaranteed; it was necessary to make sure that the music didn’t stop, causing the entire industry to crash down with it

And so all of this is very important context for why Huang’s relationship with a Chinese asset, an individual who may have been using her relationship to Huang to help get chips into China via export loopholes, why that didn’t immediately sink Huang
Many, like The Economist , called for his resignation
This wasn’t just a national-security issue; this was an affair with an Nvidia client
But in some cases, Nvidia was just believed as too big to fail
And Huang, who is the leader, with no clear successor, was needed to ensure that the AI boom could move onward, so that the numbers could keep going up
On Wednesday, news broke in the Times that Huang had had a second affair , this time with an Nvidia employee who was a direct report
And what was framed by some defenders earlier as just a slip-up, or this human dalliance, it became a pattern
A display of real recklessness, and a sign that the indiscretions of the company’s leader was too much to bear
Colette Cress, who is Nvidia’s chief financial officer, will serve as interim CEO
But this is—make no mistakes—unprecedented territory
Earlier this week on an episode of Radio Atlantic , I was asked what the nightmare scenario would be: not just for Nvidia, but for the economy in general
And I said that it would be that Jensen Huang was no longer the CEO of Nvidia
Because Jensen Huang isn’t just somebody who is a big part of this company or helped found it
He is the person who allocates where all of the chips go

title: Biden: I Was Right to Seek Reelection
excerpt: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
body: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
J oe Biden has a favorite saying that he has attributed to various family members over the years, most often to his mother: Joey , she’d tell him, never bow; never bend; never kneel; never yield

That sentiment runs through his nearly 500-page memoir, as he recounts his four years as president, his decision to run for reelection, and his attempt to stay in the race after the worst presidential-debate performance in American history. “Today there is no shortage of people who think I blindly raced to run again
Unaware of the concerns about my age,” he states, accurately. “I knew better than anyone how old I was
I knew what I was—and wasn’t—capable of doing
I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job
And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities.” Biden, as you can tell, is neither reflective nor repentant
He does not concede mistakes, and seems to regret almost nothing

He believes he was right to run for a second term, wishes he had been given the chance for a second debate with Donald Trump, and still insists he maintained the support of average voters even as party leadership pressed him to get out of the race
Evidence to the contrary never intrudes on Biden’s recounting of his last acts in politics after a half-century-long career

To make the case that his debate debacle should not have been disqualifying, he notes that Barack Obama had had a “terrible” outing during his first debate in 2012 and had left it to his vice president to “stop the bleeding
Which I did.” The argument may strain credulity, but it is quintessentially Biden
Several books have covered this ground—including Jill Biden’s View From the East Wing , which was released in June
But Joe Biden’s memoir, Promise Me, America , is the fullest account of his thinking in his own words
One of the most revealing passages comes in the last third of the book, after Biden narrates key episodes of his presidency

With Trump the likely Republican nominee, Biden comes up with a very Trumpian justification for why he needed to run against him, with echoes of Trump’s 2016 vow, “I alone can fix it”: “I believed I was the best person to do it
I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump
And I felt I was the best person to do it again.” Biden is aware of the second-guessing that arose from that choice
He just doesn’t give it any credence. “I had asked the hard questions of myself
Could I do it? Did I still want to do it? Was there anyone else to do it?” he writes. “I answered that yes, physically I would be able to do the job
And not only did I want to do it, I wanted to do it more than ever.” Yet he also suggests his decision to run was selfless, not selfish

He may have openly coveted the presidency for most of his life, but he insists that a single term would have been satisfactory. “The easiest thing for me to do would have been to say I wouldn’t run again
It would have been far easier for me, and for my family

I felt I had set the country on the right path.” And he had, in fact, defeated Trump in 2020, winning what he termed a “battle for the soul of this nation,” and the first half of the book is a reminder of some of the sweeping legislation that he shepherded through Congress
The decisions he made four years later, though, helped Trump return to political power
It is no small irony that the book is coming out during a moment of Democratic jubilation, one in which the party seems eager to move beyond what it once was
But now Democrats are being visited by a Ghost of the Party’s Past
The book is a reminder of the painful intramural debates that marked an ultimately failed attempt to hold the presidency
It is also a reminder of how stubborn Biden remains, how the man who always felt burned and resentful of Democrats who overlooked him still has some scores to settle
His voice had thinned, and he had a tendency of misstating places and names
But his gait, in particular, had become such a visual reminder of his age that it came up when Mitt Romney and his family were over at the White House in May 2022 for a private tour
The senator pulled the president aside for a quiet moment. “Pump your arms,” Romney told him. “Excuse me?” Biden responded. “You’re holding your hands stiffly by your side when you walk
Pump your arms and you’ll look more energetic and confident,” Romney instructed
Biden thought it was good advice—delivered via the long-lost art of bipartisan decency—and he tried to take it

But it also became an example of Biden’s reluctance to see his age and cognitive decline as a reason he couldn’t run for reelection, as if pumping his arms vigorously enough might cause voters to overlook his aging body and mind. “I believed the experience and the wisdom I had gained over fifty years in public life outweighed the obvious weaknesses of age,” he writes. [ Read: A different kind of fading president ] He points to two moments that convinced him he could run again

The first was his 2023 State of the Union address, which he says received “universal, enthusiastic support from my fellow Democrats.” The second was his unannounced trip to Kyiv two weeks later—a risky foray into a war zone but one that, in Biden’s telling, included packed PB&J sandwiches and, as a longtime Amtrak rider, a fascination with Ukraine’s rail system
He felt that he had addressed concerns that he lacked the vigor to run for reelection
He recounts his advisers being in agreement before his April 2023 announcement that he was running again, during a “speak now or forever hold your peace” meeting in the Treaty Room
Ron Klain sat on the couch next to him, Jen O’Malley Dillon nearby
Jill Biden urged everyone to give their unvarnished views

title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
excerpt: Brain implant volunteers want more respect: Ian Burkhart, who had a brain implant for seven-and-a-half years, helped develop new guidelines pushing for trial pa
body: Brain implant volunteers want more respect: Ian Burkhart, who had a brain implant for seven-and-a-half years, helped develop new guidelines pushing for trial participants to have the option to be recognized as genuine research collaborators and listed as coauthors on scientific papers

Your brain data should be yours: The guidelines argue that participants' neural data is personal information, and that NDAs or embargoes should not block someone from sharing their own brain data with their doctor
Losing an implant can feel like losing a limb: When funding dried up or companies collapsed, participants like Burkhart lost devices—and abilities—with little warning

The guidelines call for researchers to fund and plan removals carefully, giving participants real time to prepare " data-chronoton-post-id="1148474" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades

Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.” The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart , who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014
He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs)
Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist

But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.” Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old
Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control
He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement
The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head
Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it
The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits

Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.” In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition —an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers
Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences
The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy
The guidelines, published on Tuesday , lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories
One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants

During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.” As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t
He says he was a key member of the research team
Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says
Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.   The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy

That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention
In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants
Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data
Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data
Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement

But people who have brain implants designed for turning thoughts into words might feel differently.  The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors. “It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.” The guidelines also address what comes after a trial
Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some issues with funding

When we last spoke a few years ago , he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about brain surgery here.) Ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp
But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again
Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has said she felt she “became one” with her implant
When the company that made it went bust two years later, the device was removed against her will —an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights
Researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines
Participants should be given plenty of time to prepare for the surgery to remove it
And researchers should set aside extra funds to support trial participants who have to do that
Some of the guidelines are vague and may overlap with existing ethics standards
They don’t all spell out explicit solutions
They were also developed with feedback from a small group of individuals—the number of people living with BCIs is still very low
The team hopes to grow and expand on the guidelines over time

title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
excerpt: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the
body: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future

Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results
And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda
Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision

Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers , the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor
And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs
For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape

Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.  What were they thinking? The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us
Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election

Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC
But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else
In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment
Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die

Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind

In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of

Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “ violence and death to our enemies ” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”? I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all
Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology
The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand

There’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “ masculine energy ,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10
Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration
Instead, Big Tech tied itself to Trump and made its most important goals and investments—many related to grid access and data center permits—immediate targets for Democrats
In tech, you can always sunset a feature or update some code
But in politics, there is no undo button for failures that change public perception
The tech elites’ decision to visibly align their businesses with a temporary movement has left them no credible way to pivot now that the climate has changed
As one Meta employee who has worked closely with Zuckerberg put it, “Mark is a long-term thinker, but he never charts a plan of how to get there

It’s spray and pray and see what happens.” As for whether employees expect the company to do a strategic postmortem? “Facebook has never really done that.” “Move fast and break things” might work in a startup, but it’s a terrible strategy for building reputational goodwill
Previous technological leaps, like the rollout of fiber-optic technology and wireless infrastructure, avoided partisan politics
But by kowtowing to the Trump administration, Silicon Valley made artificial intelligence a culture-war issue
Now, when citizens vote on data center proposals from California to Florida , they are no longer considering only technical or economic concerns, but political ones

Tech leaders didn’t see this coming because they were too focused on the urgency of the AI race to understand how reputational damage could undermine the intangible goodwill—and ultimately the very tangible infrastructure—necessary to win it
The industry’s misreading of the moment has already punctured one myth Silicon Valley holds dear: that its leaders can always see what’s next
Aaron Zamost is a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square.

title: Why the Microsoft 365 outage is different and why it takes so long to restore email services
url:
<title>Why the Microsoft 365 outage is different and why it takes so long to restore email services</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771879/original/file-20261113-64-bdm55b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C41%2C3000%2C1999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Microsoft was a source of frustration for computer users when it stopped working on Nov. 12, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Microsoft365Outage/d6d2e197092e47079b89df8d583ddd28/photo">AP Photo/Michel Euler</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The <a href="https://apnews.com/article/microsoft-outage-outlook-email-365-status-down-d92547a821930290db2964388016979a">Microsoft services outage</a> that began on Nov. 12, 2026, is not like other internet outages. The failure affected the <a href="https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/what-is-microsoft-365">Microsoft 365</a> suite of productivity services, including the video conferencing and collaboration platform Teams, AI assistant Copilot and, significantly, the Outlook email service.</p>

<p>Microsoft <a href="https://x.com/MSFT365Status/status/2121246073955962896">reported on Nov. 13</a> that the company is “continuing to see improvements in service availability” but that “some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery.”</p>

<p>Despite decades of <a href="https://www.wired.com/2014/01/next-big-thing-missed-facebook-co-founder-says-email/">predictions about its decline</a>, email remains a <a href="https://www.emailtooltester.com/en/blog/how-many-emails-are-sent-per-day/">central pillar</a> of how organizations function. Password resets, invoices, legal notices and cybersecurity incident response coordination all depend on it. The Microsoft 365 outage <a href="https://www.wsj.com/tech/microsoft-working-to-fix-widespread-outage-8df67a4e?mod=hp_lead_pos1">affected businesses, governments and schools</a> around the world.</p>

<p>When most people think about <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-cloud-service-outages-ripple-across-the-internet-and-the-economy-272241">cloud outages</a>, they picture a broken website or a stalled app. When the service going down includes email, however, the mechanics of the failure and how to recover from it are different from those of almost every other cloud service.</p>

<p>Unlike modern web apps or authentication gatekeepers, email wasn’t designed to fail fast, meaning to immediately halt when a problem arises.</p>



<h2>Old architecture</h2>

<p>When a typical <a href="https://theconversation.com/massive-it-outage-spotlights-major-vulnerabilities-in-the-global-information-ecosystem-235155">cloud service breaks</a>, it acts like a closed door. If an authentication provider or a cloud application goes down, users are immediately locked out and see an error message. Access stops. When people cannot get into the system, they are not actively generating new work or adding heavy processing loads to the broken servers. Once engineers fix the underlying bug and unlock the door, traffic can resume and the service often recovers fairly quickly. </p>

<p>Email does not have a closed door. It is built on an older, decentralized <a href="https://youtu.be/x28ciavQ4mI">“store-and-forward” architecture</a> designed to never lose a message, even when the destination is unreachable.</p>

<p>Because email is a network of thousands of independent systems, an outage at one major provider does not stop users on other platforms from hitting “send.” During major email disruptions like the one that hit Microsoft, millions of outside users on Gmail, corporate servers or other platforms could still compose and send emails to affected accounts without seeing an immediate error message.</p>

<p>From the sender’s perspective, everything works normally. Their email provider accepts the message, attempts to hand it off to the downed provider, realizes the destination isn’t answering, and quietly holds onto the message in an outbound queue to try again later.</p>

<h2>Major highway crash</h2>

<p>One way to think about email traffic in outages is to imagine a multilane interstate highway where an accident blocks two lanes of traffic. Drivers miles away don’t stop leaving their driveways just because there is a wreck up ahead; they keep entering the highway system. Soon, traffic backs up so severely that metered on-ramps have to stop letting new cars merge onto the interstate. Before long, that gridlock spills backward onto local feeder roads and city streets, choking traffic miles away from the actual crash site.</p>

<p>In this analogy, a downed email provider is the crash. Every other email server around the world is an on-ramp or a feeder road. While the outage lasts, millions of messages continue to pile up in queues across the internet, with unaffected servers repeatedly resending email to see whether traffic is moving yet.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="a highway traffic jam" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">It takes time to get traffic moving after an accident has been cleared.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/october-2026-bavaria-ottersried-a-traffic-jam-has-formed-on-news-photo/2297443645">Pia Bayer/picture alliance via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>When engineers finally fix the root cause of an email outage, it is the equivalent of tow trucks clearing the wreckage from the highway. The road is technically open again, but traffic does not instantly return to normal speed.</p>

<p>First, the massive backlog of vehicles already stuck on the main highway has to start moving. Only after that congestion clears can the on-ramps start letting queued-up cars merge back in, which in turn slowly relieves the gridlock on the surrounding local roads. </p>

<p>Similarly, when a major email provider comes back online, it is immediately hit with a tidal wave of pent-up messages and retry attempts from every other mail server on the internet. Processing those queues without overwhelming the newly restored servers takes time – typically hours to days. </p>

<h2>Long, bumpy road to recovery</h2>

<p>Because organizations have largely outsourced their email to a small number of global providers, an outage doesn’t just disrupt one company; it <a href="https://www.reuters.com/technology/microsoft-365-outlook-down-thousands-us-users-downdetector-shows-2026-11-12/">can stall entire sectors</a> at once, cutting off the communication tool teams rely on to coordinate their emergency response. </p>

<p>And for everyday users, this unique architecture explains why email failures feel so drawn out: Even hours after a provider officially announces a problem is fixed, messages can still arrive out of order or trickle in slowly as the digital traffic jam finally clears.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296628/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

    <summary>When one email service goes down, others don’t stop trying to send emails to users of the affected service. The result is snarled traffic that takes time to clear up.</summary>
    <author>
      <name>Doug Jacobson, University Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Iowa State University</name>

body: Microsoft was a source of frustration for computer users when it stopped working on Nov. 12, 2026
AP Photo/Michel Euler The Microsoft services outage that began on Nov. 12, 2026, is not like other internet outages

The failure affected the Microsoft 365 suite of productivity services, including the video conferencing and collaboration platform Teams, AI assistant Copilot and, significantly, the Outlook email service

Microsoft reported on Nov. 13 that the company is “continuing to see improvements in service availability” but that “some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery.” Despite decades of predictions about its decline , email remains a central pillar of how organizations function
Password resets, invoices, legal notices and cybersecurity incident response coordination all depend on it
The Microsoft 365 outage affected businesses, governments and schools around the world
When most people think about cloud outages , they picture a broken website or a stalled app
When the service going down includes email, however, the mechanics of the failure and how to recover from it are different from those of almost every other cloud service
Unlike modern web apps or authentication gatekeepers, email wasn’t designed to fail fast, meaning to immediately halt when a problem arises
Old architecture When a typical cloud service breaks , it acts like a closed door
If an authentication provider or a cloud application goes down, users are immediately locked out and see an error message
When people cannot get into the system, they are not actively generating new work or adding heavy processing loads to the broken servers
Once engineers fix the underlying bug and unlock the door, traffic can resume and the service often recovers fairly quickly
It is built on an older, decentralized “store-and-forward” architecture designed to never lose a message, even when the destination is unreachable

Because email is a network of thousands of independent systems, an outage at one major provider does not stop users on other platforms from hitting “send.” During major email disruptions like the one that hit Microsoft, millions of outside users on Gmail, corporate servers or other platforms could still compose and send emails to affected accounts without seeing an immediate error message
From the sender’s perspective, everything works normally

Their email provider accepts the message, attempts to hand it off to the downed provider, realizes the destination isn’t answering, and quietly holds onto the message in an outbound queue to try again later
Major highway crash One way to think about email traffic in outages is to imagine a multilane interstate highway where an accident blocks two lanes of traffic
Drivers miles away don’t stop leaving their driveways just because there is a wreck up ahead; they keep entering the highway system
Soon, traffic backs up so severely that metered on-ramps have to stop letting new cars merge onto the interstate
Before long, that gridlock spills backward onto local feeder roads and city streets, choking traffic miles away from the actual crash site
In this analogy, a downed email provider is the crash
Every other email server around the world is an on-ramp or a feeder road
While the outage lasts, millions of messages continue to pile up in queues across the internet, with unaffected servers repeatedly resending email to see whether traffic is moving yet
It takes time to get traffic moving after an accident has been cleared
Pia Bayer/picture alliance via Getty Images When engineers finally fix the root cause of an email outage, it is the equivalent of tow trucks clearing the wreckage from the highway
The road is technically open again, but traffic does not instantly return to normal speed
First, the massive backlog of vehicles already stuck on the main highway has to start moving
Only after that congestion clears can the on-ramps start letting queued-up cars merge back in, which in turn slowly relieves the gridlock on the surrounding local roads
Similarly, when a major email provider comes back online, it is immediately hit with a tidal wave of pent-up messages and retry attempts from every other mail server on the internet
Processing those queues without overwhelming the newly restored servers takes time – typically hours to days

Long, bumpy road to recovery Because organizations have largely outsourced their email to a small number of global providers, an outage doesn’t just disrupt one company; it can stall entire sectors at once, cutting off the communication tool teams rely on to coordinate their emergency response

And for everyday users, this unique architecture explains why email failures feel so drawn out: Even hours after a provider officially announces a problem is fixed, messages can still arrive out of order or trickle in slowly as the digital traffic jam finally clears
