<title>Oceans and forests have absorbed roughly half our carbon emissions for decades, slowing climate change – but can they keep it up?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771728/original/file-20261112-64-s1kp6w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C5%2C8106%2C5404&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Oceans and land have been absorbing a lot of the carbon emissions humans create.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/pistol-river-sunrise-royalty-free-image/1191054726?phrase=highway%20traffic%20ocean&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Dean Fikar/Moment via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Over the past two centuries, humans have pumped billions of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere <a href="https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-3211-2026">by burning fossil fuels</a>, raising global temperatures in the process.</p>

<p>Luckily for humanity, Earth has done what it could to soften the impact.</p>

<p>The world’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed9544">oceans have absorbed 35%</a> of carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels since 1990, our new research shows, and the forests and other plants of the world have absorbed another 13%.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A wave breaking." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The oceans absorb a large amount of humanity’s carbon dioxide emissions from burning fossil fuels. That amount has been increasing, but new research suggests the increase will slow in the coming decades.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/a-large-ocean-wave-crests-and-breaks-vYc1k5x_f7I">Joachim Lesne/Unsplash</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The importance of these two enormous <a href="https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/carbon-sources-and-sinks/">natural carbon sinks</a> cannot be overstated as global temperatures rise, <a href="https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-11/">fueling heat waves, fires, storms, floods and droughts</a> around the world. Yet there is much that scientists do not understand about these carbon sinks – most importantly, how exactly they’ll behave in the future.</p>

<p>If the oceans and forests keep absorbing the same amount of carbon dioxide, scientists will have a sense of what to expect in the future and what can be done to slow climate change. And governments will know their <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-023-01848-5">remaining carbon budgets</a> – that is, how much carbon dioxide can still be emitted into the atmosphere while keeping global temperatures below agreed-to levels.</p>

<p>But what if those carbon sinks change?</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="View of thick trees in a rainforest" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Earth’s forests take in large amounts of carbon dioxide. But they can also become carbon sources, especially if the climate continues to change.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/green-trees-under-white-sky-during-daytime-C6GmjaUWmBU">Crystal Mirallegro/Unsplash</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>We have been working on greenhouse gas measurements for decades. In a new study, published Nov. 12, 2026, in the journal Science, we describe an <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed9544">alternative method for measuring</a> these crucial carbon sinks, and what it shows.</p>

<p>We found that while the ocean sink has been expanding, meaning the oceans are taking in more carbon dioxide, that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed9544">expansion might begin to slow down</a>, leaving the oceans less effective at absorbing carbon in the coming decades. We found that the land sink has not been expanding, which was something of a surprise.</p>

<h2>The fiendishly difficult task of measuring carbon sinks</h2>

<p>Measuring how much carbon is being taken up by the world’s oceans and forests is devilishly difficult and prohibitively expensive.</p>

<p>This is because many parts of the land and ocean don’t behave in the same ways. What occurs in one ocean region or forest can be very different from another; and the behavior in one year can be very different in the next, often for reasons scientists do not fully understand.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-9-1937-2016">Computer models</a> can help overcome some of these complexities, but they too have limitations. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2021RG000736">Satellites</a> can also help, but they cannot see through clouds, nor can they see what is happening in the soil or mid-to-deep ocean.</p>



<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Line chart comparing ocean sink, land sink, and fossil fuel emissions" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=428&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=428&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=428&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=538&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=538&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=538&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The 10-year running averages for the two global carbon sinks – land and ocean – show the ocean absorbing much more, but that increase in how much it absorbs is slowing. The land sink does not show an increasing trend in recent decades.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://scrippso2.ucsd.edu/">Figure adapted from Morgan et al., Science, 2026; atmospheric CO2 data from NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory; atmospheric O2 data from Scripps Institution of Oceanography</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>As carbon cycle scientists, we set out to find a different way to measure these carbon sinks.</p>

<p>Our new study approaches the problem from another angle. We used <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-08-095975-7.00420-4">high-precision measurements of atmospheric oxygen</a> (O₂), combined with <a href="https://gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends/global.html">atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) measurements</a>, to quantify how the ocean and land carbon sinks takeing up carbon dioxide.</p>

<p>This works because land, oceans and burning fossil fuels have different effects on oxygen: When fossil fuels are burned, they not only produce CO₂, they consume O₂. On land, when plants take up CO₂ to grow, they simultaneously release O₂. When the oceans take up atmospheric CO₂, there is no corresponding release of O₂.</p>

<p>This means that if we measure both CO₂ and O₂ in the atmosphere, then we can quantify the ocean and land carbon sinks. It is a straightforward mathematical approach of solving two equations with two unknowns, combined with our knowledge and measurements of the global budgets of CO₂ and O₂.</p>

<h2>What we found</h2>

<p>When we looked at the ocean and land carbon sinks over the past three decades, the results were surprising and sobering.</p>

<p>In contrast to most <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-023-00456-3">computer model simulations</a>, we did not find the land carbon sink increasing over time to keep pace with increasing fossil fuel emissions. We did, however, find a larger ocean carbon sink than <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2023GB007780">predicted by most models</a>, and we found that it has been increasing as emissions grow.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Line charts showing differences among models and methods." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=252&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=252&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=252&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The 10-year running averages for the two global carbon sinks – land and ocean – show the ocean absorbing much more, but that increase in how much it absorbs is slowing. The land sink does not show an increasing trend in recent decades.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed9544">Adapted from Morgan et al., Science, 2026, supplementary materials.</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Where is the climate headed?</h2>

<p>If these trends in carbon sinks continue, then in the coming decades, humans will be relying more heavily on the oceans to slow down climate change. But in the next few decades, there are reasons to believe the oceans could become less effective at absorbing carbon.</p>

<p>For example, warmer waters are <a href="https://news.wisc.edu/climate-change-reducing-oceans-carbon-dioxide-uptake/">not able to hold as much gas</a>, such as carbon dioxide. Warmer surface waters are also less efficient at <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/oceans-carbon-balance/">mixing into the deep ocean</a>, which has the beneficial effect of locking carbon dioxide away from the atmosphere for many hundreds of years. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="View under the surface of the ocean" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Warmer waters can’t hold as much carbon dioxide or mix as well with lower ocean layers.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/clear-blue-body-of-water-XexawgzYOBc">Cristian Palmer/Unsplash</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The data for the past decade hints at the possibility that while the ocean carbon sink is increasing now, its rate of increase may be slowing down.</p>

<h2>Carbon cycle models need to improve</h2>

<p>For the oceans, most computer models agree with each other, but, for the historical period, they do not match our oxygen-based results. For the land, models vary widely from each other, and most do not match our oxygen-based results.</p>

<p>Computer models are essential to provide governments with feasible scenarios to avoid dangerous climate change, but to be effective they need to be better grounded in what real-world observations are showing. Nature is difficult to represent with a series of equations, and observations are few considering the size of the planet.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/dXBzFNEwoj8?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">How scientists measure carbon dioxide and oxygen in the atmosphere. UCSD.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Looking ahead</h2>

<p>We believe our study improves <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed9544">understanding of global carbon sinks</a> and can help lead to more reliable projections of what might happen with climate change in the coming decades. But like any scientific approach, our oxygen method also has drawbacks.</p>

<p>The measurements themselves are challenging, such that only about 10 research laboratories in the world are routinely doing them. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1600-0889.2006.00196.x">Calibrating the measurements</a> is an ongoing challenge. Earth is not helping: Warmer waters hold less gas, meaning that as oceans warm in response to climate change, they <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-018-0152-2">expel some oxygen into the atmosphere</a>. We must account for this in our carbon sink calculations. excerpt: Oceans and land have been absorbing a lot of the carbon emissions humans create
body: Oceans and land have been absorbing a lot of the carbon emissions humans create

Dean Fikar/Moment via Getty Images Over the past two centuries, humans have pumped billions of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere by burning fossil fuels , raising global temperatures in the process
Luckily for humanity, Earth has done what it could to soften the impact
The world’s oceans have absorbed 35% of carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels since 1990, our new research shows, and the forests and other plants of the world have absorbed another 13%
The oceans absorb a large amount of humanity’s carbon dioxide emissions from burning fossil fuels
That amount has been increasing, but new research suggests the increase will slow in the coming decades

Joachim Lesne/Unsplash , CC BY The importance of these two enormous natural carbon sinks cannot be overstated as global temperatures rise, fueling heat waves, fires, storms, floods and droughts around the world
Yet there is much that scientists do not understand about these carbon sinks – most importantly, how exactly they’ll behave in the future
If the oceans and forests keep absorbing the same amount of carbon dioxide, scientists will have a sense of what to expect in the future and what can be done to slow climate change
And governments will know their remaining carbon budgets – that is, how much carbon dioxide can still be emitted into the atmosphere while keeping global temperatures below agreed-to levels
But what if those carbon sinks change? Earth’s forests take in large amounts of carbon dioxide
But they can also become carbon sources, especially if the climate continues to change
Crystal Mirallegro/Unsplash , CC BY We have been working on greenhouse gas measurements for decades
In a new study, published Nov. 12, 2026, in the journal Science, we describe an alternative method for measuring these crucial carbon sinks, and what it shows

We found that while the ocean sink has been expanding, meaning the oceans are taking in more carbon dioxide, that expansion might begin to slow down , leaving the oceans less effective at absorbing carbon in the coming decades
We found that the land sink has not been expanding, which was something of a surprise
The fiendishly difficult task of measuring carbon sinks Measuring how much carbon is being taken up by the world’s oceans and forests is devilishly difficult and prohibitively expensive
This is because many parts of the land and ocean don’t behave in the same ways
What occurs in one ocean region or forest can be very different from another; and the behavior in one year can be very different in the next, often for reasons scientists do not fully understand
Computer models can help overcome some of these complexities, but they too have limitations
Satellites can also help, but they cannot see through clouds, nor can they see what is happening in the soil or mid-to-deep ocean
The 10-year running averages for the two global carbon sinks – land and ocean – show the ocean absorbing much more, but that increase in how much it absorbs is slowing
The land sink does not show an increasing trend in recent decades

Figure adapted from Morgan et al., Science, 2026; atmospheric CO2 data from NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory; atmospheric O2 data from Scripps Institution of Oceanography As carbon cycle scientists, we set out to find a different way to measure these carbon sinks
Our new study approaches the problem from another angle
We used high-precision measurements of atmospheric oxygen (O₂), combined with atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) measurements , to quantify how the ocean and land carbon sinks takeing up carbon dioxide
This works because land, oceans and burning fossil fuels have different effects on oxygen: When fossil fuels are burned, they not only produce CO₂, they consume O₂
On land, when plants take up CO₂ to grow, they simultaneously release O₂
When the oceans take up atmospheric CO₂, there is no corresponding release of O₂
This means that if we measure both CO₂ and O₂ in the atmosphere, then we can quantify the ocean and land carbon sinks
It is a straightforward mathematical approach of solving two equations with two unknowns, combined with our knowledge and measurements of the global budgets of CO₂ and O₂
What we found When we looked at the ocean and land carbon sinks over the past three decades, the results were surprising and sobering
In contrast to most computer model simulations , we did not find the land carbon sink increasing over time to keep pace with increasing fossil fuel emissions
We did, however, find a larger ocean carbon sink than predicted by most models , and we found that it has been increasing as emissions grow
The 10-year running averages for the two global carbon sinks – land and ocean – show the ocean absorbing much more, but that increase in how much it absorbs is slowing
The land sink does not show an increasing trend in recent decades
Adapted from Morgan et al., Science, 2026, supplementary materials
Where is the climate headed? If these trends in carbon sinks continue, then in the coming decades, humans will be relying more heavily on the oceans to slow down climate change
But in the next few decades, there are reasons to believe the oceans could become less effective at absorbing carbon
For example, warmer waters are not able to hold as much gas , such as carbon dioxide

title: To get Americans to care about climate change, just call it climate change

<title>To get Americans to care about climate change, just call it climate change</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771438/original/file-20261111-64-wch55q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1692%2C1128&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Escalating the language might work in a rally, but the general public isn&#39;t as swayed by it, studies show.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/participants-seen-holding-signs-at-the-protest-ahead-of-the-news-photo/1675096474">Erik McGregor/LightRocket via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>You may be hearing phrases like “climate crisis,” “climate emergency” and “climate justice” a lot as the 2026 United Nations climate summit is underway. Political leaders, including <a href="https://unfccc.int/news/transcript-of-remarks-made-by-un-secretary-general-antonio-guterres-to-the-cop31-leaders-summit">U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres</a>, are using them to try to get across the urgent risks and consequences of climate change. The <a href="https://www.wri.org/insights/2023-ipcc-ar6-synthesis-report-climate-change-findings">danger is real</a>, but is using this language actually persuasive?</p>

<p>It turns out that Americans are more familiar with – and more concerned about – climate change and global warming than they are about climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice, according to a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-024-03786-3">survey we conducted</a> with a nationally representative sample of 5,137 Americans.</p>

<p>Moreover, we found no evidence that the alternative terms increased people’s sense of urgency, willingness to support climate-friendly policies or willingness to act.</p>

<p>The familiar terms – climate change and global warming – did at least as well, and sometimes better, than climate crisis and climate emergency in eliciting concern, perceived urgency and willingness to act. The phrase climate justice consistently tended to do worse, likely in part because it was the least familiar. These response patterns were similar among Republicans, Democrats and independents.</p>



<h2>Just keep it simple</h2>

<p>In our work as <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=JjiiTkcAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">research</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=VBvoFacAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">psychologists</a>, we have explored how Americans respond to the ways climate change is communicated and have uncovered a need to use straightforward language.</p>

<p>For example, people we interviewed for a study published in 2021 felt that climate experts were <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-021-03183-0">talking over their heads</a> with terms like “adaptation,” “mitigation,” “sustainability” and “carbon-dioxide removal.” They wanted experts to use more familiar terms instead. </p>

<p><iframe id="LecWo" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/LecWo/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0"></iframe></p>

<p>This inspired us to write a <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-quick-guide-to-climate-change-jargon-what-experts-mean-by-mitigation-carbon-neutral-and-6-other-key-terms-167172">quick guide to climate jargon</a>, published in The Conversation. Using everyday language makes information easier to understand, and even highly educated people tend to prefer it.</p>

<p>Jargon like “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s44185-026-00163-4">biodiversity loss</a>” has similar problems. That refers to the shrinking variety of life on Earth, which is exacerbated by climate change. A survey of 7,338 U.S. adults led by one of us found people were much more familiar with and more concerned about “extinction of plants and animals” – or, if an explanation was provided, “nature loss”. </p>

<p>Even with an explanation, “biodiversity loss” was the least familiar and of least concern for people among several terms. Most people didn’t find “biodiversity crisis” or “extinction crisis” familiar either. </p>

<p>Yet, experts often use complex jargon because it is familiar to them, and they may not realize it is unfamiliar to others.</p>

<h2>How the terms evolved</h2>

<p>It has become common to talk about climate change and global warming as if they have the same meaning, but <a href="https://www.ipcc.ch/sr15/chapter/glossary/">there are differences</a>. Climate change refers to changes in the overall climate, while global warming refers specifically to rising temperatures.</p>

<p>A <a href="https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315687391">historical review</a> found that, in the past, people were less likely to associate the term climate change with the idea that humans are actively warming the planet than they were with the term global warming. Perhaps this is why <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-011-0070-4">Democrats used to like the term global warming,</a> while the popularization of the term climate change has been <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2003/03/02/us/a-call-for-softer-greener-language.html">credited to Frank Luntz</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315687391">an adviser to the George W. Bush</a> administration.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-010-9882-x">Past surveys</a> also found that Democrats used to think of global warming as being more serious than climate change, while Republicans thought of climate change as more serious than global warming. But <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvp.2020.101414">according to a recent review</a>, these partisan differences have now faded.</p>

<p><iframe id="IaVVC" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/IaVVC/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0"></iframe></p>

<p>Alternative terms such as climate crisis, climate emergency and climate justice have been used to emphasize other aspects of climate change and to try to raise concern. In 2019, the British newspaper <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2019/may/17/why-the-guardian-is-changing-the-language-it-uses-about-the-environment">The Guardian</a> switched to using climate crisis and climate emergency because it wanted to convey urgency.</p>

<p>Activists use the term climate justice to draw attention to climate change as a human rights challenge: Low-income people around the world <a href="https://theconversation.com/heat-waves-hit-the-poor-hardest-calculating-the-rising-impact-on-those-least-able-to-adapt-to-the-warming-climate-175224">suffer the most</a> from the effects of climate change, despite being the least responsible for causing it.</p>

<h2>The takeaway: Avoid overheated language</h2>

<p>Right now, the terms climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice are less familiar and elicit less concern than climate change or global warming.</p>

<p>Even if these terms become more commonplace, there is no guarantee that they will heighten concern or inspire action. In fact, studies have suggested that phrases like climate crisis <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/1533015X.2013.795836">could backfire</a> if they don’t resonate with people.</p>

<p>Our advice: Don’t make the mistake of using overheated language. Just stick with familiar terms that people understand – use global warming when referring to rising temperatures and climate change for overall changes in the climate.</p>

<p><em>This updates an article originally published <a href="https://theconversation.com/if-you-want-americans-to-pay-attention-to-climate-change-just-call-it-climate-change-235002">Aug. 12, 2024</a>, with a new study and discussions at the 2026 U.N. climate conference, COP31.</em></p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296481/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>Wändi Bruine de Bruin has received funding for this research from University of Southern California’s Wrigley Institute for Environmental Studies, the Golden Belt Community Foundation and Lloyd&#39;s Register Foundation.</span></em></p><p class="fine-print"><em><span>Gale Sinatra received funding from the National Science Foundation.</span></em></p></content>

title: Debate in New York City over city-run groceries is not just about food, but something bigger
url:
<title>Debate in New York City over city-run groceries is not just about food, but something bigger</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771653/original/file-20261112-64-qfy0aq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6602%2C4401&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Five city-run groceries in a city of 8 million won&#39;t substantially lower food prices, but the experiment might cause shoppers to think differently about the role of government.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/new-york-city-mayor-zohran-mamdani-holds-up-bananas-as-he-news-photo/2287861148?phrase=Mamdani%20grocery&amp;adppopup=true">Spencer Platt/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. <a href="https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/05/mayor-mamdani-announces-the-peninsula-in-the-bronx-as-the-second">Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026</a> that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow. </p>

<p>Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with <a href="https://www.nyc.gov/assets/foodpolicy/downloads/pdf/NYC-Food-by-the-Numbers-2025.pdf">nearly 1,000 supermarkets</a> and more than <a href="https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/newyorkcitynewyork">8 million inhabitants</a>. But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices.</p>

<p>Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/nyc-grocers-sue-city-over-subsidized-municipal-grocery-stores-plan/">independent grocers</a>, <a href="https://www.grocerydive.com/news/new-york-city-municipal-grocery-stores-lawsuit-multicultural-business-coalition/828660/">supermarket trade associations</a> and a <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/nyc-city-run-grocery-store-lawsuit/">coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses</a>. </p>

<p>What explains this pushback?</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=VBgW-tsAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">food policy scholar</a>, I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs. </p>

<p>The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has <a href="https://www.vitalcitynyc.org/government-is-already-in-the-grocery-business/">not operated independently of government</a>. In fact, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-publhealth-052220-021059">public policies and investments</a> have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food. </p>

<p>It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see.</p>

<p>That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly. </p>

<p>If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A man wearing in a turban and pushing a dolly walks by a grocery store in the Queens neighborhood of Jackson Heights, which has a large South Asian community." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771743/original/file-20261112-64-ecse3m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771743/original/file-20261112-64-ecse3m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=405&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771743/original/file-20261112-64-ecse3m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=405&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771743/original/file-20261112-64-ecse3m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=405&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771743/original/file-20261112-64-ecse3m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=509&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771743/original/file-20261112-64-ecse3m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=509&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771743/original/file-20261112-64-ecse3m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=509&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Some immigrant owners of New York grocery stores have warned that city-run alternatives will undercut them.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/general-views-of-the-indian-community-of-the-jackson-news-photo/53089295?phrase=indian%20grocery%20store%20new%20york&amp;adppopup=true">Scott Gries/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>How the plan will work</h2>

<p>New York City has <a href="https://edc.nyc/program/nyc-groceries">committed US$70 million</a> to develop these stores, which will be open to all.</p>

<p>While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced <a href="https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/07/transcript-_mayor-mamdani-unveils-30--discount---including-all-p">30% below</a> typical retail prices. </p>

<p>In this respect, the stores offer a “<a href="https://democracyjournal.org/magazine/56/reviving-public-action/">public option</a>” – a <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/politics-policy-and-public-options/78B6D051FD7EEF9990D289CCE61EEE2F">government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives</a>, like public schools and city hospitals. </p>

<p>Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable.</p>

<p>At his <a href="https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/05/transcript--mayor-mamdani-announces-the-peninsula-in-the-bronx-a">May announcement</a>, Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.” </p>

<h2>A fresh form of intervention</h2>

<p>Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses. </p>

<p>In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1934/06/15/archives/19946-quarts-sold-of-city-milk-in-day-11151-families-get-supply-at.html">selling discounted milk</a> to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new <a href="https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/1995/05/29/the-political-supermarket">Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem</a> in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business. </p>

<p>A more recent example is the city’s <a href="https://edc.nyc/program/food-retail-expansion-support-health-fresh">Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program</a>, known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and <a href="https://www.jstor.org/content/oa_chapter_edited/j.ctv513dv1.23?seq=1">zoning incentives</a> to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods. </p>

<p>These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them. </p>

<p>FRESH is just one example of an approach toward <a href="https://ir.lawnet.fordham.edu/ulj/vol45/iss4/5/">supermarket financing</a> that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-2427.12515">blamed on a scarcity of</a> neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers. </p>

<p>Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/s1368980017000933">researchers have found</a> that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets.</p>

<p>This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare. </p>

<p>This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “<a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/S/bo12244559.html">the submerged state</a>.” </p>

<h2>Bringing the state into the open</h2>

<p>Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways. </p>

<p>First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share <a href="https://edc.nyc/press-release/nycedc-selects-branding-design-team-develop-visual-identity-nyc-groceries">distinct branding</a> so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food. </p>

<p>If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate.</p>

<p>Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable. </p>

<p>To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business. </p>

<p>Yet East Harlem’s Pathmark demonstrates that new supermarkets and smaller retailers can coexist. Between 2000 and 2015, the number of small grocery stores and bodegas in the neighborhood <a href="https://cunyurbanfoodpolicy.org/resources/report/eating-in-east-harlem/">increased from 100 to 126</a>, while supermarkets rose from 10 to 18. That said, those figures don’t establish Pathmark’s effects on individual businesses. </p>

<p>The municipal stores’ impact on nearby retailers remains an open question. But the task for New York City is to ensure that private operators deliver excellent service and real savings, and that their commercial interests don’t undermine the public mission. It will also need to provide good working conditions and track effects on nearby businesses.</p>

<p>Ultimately, public ownership doesn’t guarantee success. But it makes government’s responsibility for the outcome impossible to miss.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291749/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>MAHA suffered heavy losses in the 2026 midterms, but the movement is far from dead</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771648/original/file-20261112-64-ry5zsp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5319%2C3546&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The MAHA movement&#39;s influence in Washington remains strong, despite its political losses in the 2026 midterm elections.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/make-america-healthy-again-sign-is-displayed-outside-of-the-news-photo/2303603871">Kevin Carter/Getty Images News</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Candidates tied to the Make America Healthy Again, or MAHA, movement suffered a series of electoral <a href="https://theconversation.com/epic-blue-wave-helps-democrats-take-congress-in-overwhelming-rebuke-to-president-trump-295830">defeats</a> in the 2026 midterm elections, raising questions about MAHA’s political future.</p>

<p>Despite its name, MAHA has become a controversial force in American health politics. While the movement calls for <a href="https://www.npr.org/sections/shots-health-news/2025/07/30/nx-s1-5453714/state-laws-food-dyes-additives-maha">healthier food</a>, <a href="https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/hhs-launches-10-million-presidential-fitness-school-innovation-challenge.html">increased physical activity</a> and greater corporate transparency, prominent figures within it have also challenged established scientific evidence, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s44319-025-00639-7">especially on vaccines</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/05/end-of-maha-2026-midterms-losses-democrats-aoc-cory-booker/">Some commentators</a> and critics <a href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2026/10/23/rfk-maha-trump-alliance-calley-means/92218973007/">have</a> <a href="https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/04/midterm-health-policy-winners-losers-medicare-for-all-rfk-jr/">described</a> the defeat of MAHA-aligned candidates like <a href="https://www.thegazette.com/opinion/columnists/opinion-lahn-s-governor-bid-doomed-from-the-start/article_76de3451-45ec-4f9a-a08b-a228d9e04fad.html">Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn</a> as a “<a href="https://www.thedailybeast.com/rfk-jr-and-maha-suffer-brutal-election-night-wipeout">brutal election night wipeout</a>.” Others have asked whether MAHA is “<a href="https://arstechnica.com/health/2026/11/is-maha-dying-or-will-it-be-reborn-whats-next-after-crushing-midterm-losses/">dying</a>.”</p>

<p>Yet many Americans still support MAHA and the <a href="https://www.kff.org/public-opinion/kff-health-tracking-poll-maha-and-the-midterms/">policies it champions</a>. Its supporters also continue to hold powerful positions in the Trump administration – like Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.,  National Institutes of Health Director <a href="https://thehill.com/policy/healthcare/5748218-bhattacharya-cdc-nih-leadership-concern/">Jay Bhattacharya</a>, and <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2025/12/31/kyle-diamantas-maha-fda-food-policy-00698153">Kyle Diamantas</a>, acting commissioner of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration – even as a new Congress prepares to take office in January 2027. </p>

<p>We are <a href="https://www.robertbrehmpolitics.com/">political scientists</a> who study <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=YsnoBM8AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">public opinion on healthcare policy</a>. We see MAHA’s electoral losses as a political setback, not a death sentence. The movement’s influence extends beyond its candidates and the elections they contest.</p>





<h2>Election losses</h2>

<p>MAHA’s electoral losses came amid a potentially <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/03/voters-punish-trump-with-dramatic-swing-democrats/">generational swing toward Democrats</a> across the country, </p>

<p>More than <a href="https://arstechnica.com/health/2026/11/is-maha-dying-or-will-it-be-reborn-whats-next-after-crushing-midterm-losses/">half the 24 gubernatorial and Congressional candidates</a> endorsed by MAHA’s political action committee, <a href="https://www.mahaaction.org/about">MAHA Action</a>, lost their election bids. These included Lahn, Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton and House candidate Vic Mellor in Rhode Island. Others, like incumbent Representative Anna Paulina Luna, R-FL, <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/florida-us-house-district-13-results">won by less than 1%</a> in a district that she <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-elections/florida-us-house-district-13-results">won by nearly 10 percentage points</a> in 2024.</p>

<p>Lahn’s defeat stands out as a major loss. Lahn, a farmer who <a href="https://www.ap.org/news-highlights/elections/2026/maha-candidate-beats-trumps-choice-in-republican-primary-for-iowa-governor/">railed against pesticides</a> on the campaign trail and promised to <a href="https://iowacapitaldispatch.com/2026/10/28/zach-lahn-joins-hhs-secretary-robert-f-kennedy-jr-for-maha-rally/">ban COVID-19 vaccinations in Iowa</a>, was endorsed by Kennedy. Lahn has been described by some as a model MAHA candidate and received over <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/healthcare/articles/maha-action-pac-donates-1-123300212.html">US$1 million in campaign contributions</a> from MAHA Action. </p>

<h2>Public support remains strong</h2>

<p>But the movement’s poor showing at the ballot box does not mean that some of MAHA’s ideas are unpopular among Americans. A May 2026 poll conducted by the health policy organization KFF found that <a href="https://www.kff.org/public-opinion/kff-health-tracking-poll-maha-and-the-midterms/">41% of American adults supported MAHA</a>, including many Democrats and independents. </p>

<p>Many Americans also share MAHA’s concerns about food safety. According to KFF, 75% of Americans believe the government does too little to regulate chemical additives in food, while 64% say the same about agricultural pesticides.</p>

<p>Yet the popularity of MAHA policies did little to help MAHA-backed candidates win in the <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/10/28/nx-s1-6018272/food-health-trump-wellness-maha-rfk-jr">first election cycle</a> where MAHA-aligned candidates were on the ballot. Following the midterm elections, <a href="https://time.com/article/2026/11/05/maha-supporters-say-trump-broken-promises-helped-democrats-win/">some MAHA activists moved to blame President Donald Trump</a> for failing to fulfill promises on these issues. </p>

<p>One prime example: In a <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6205715-calley-means-susan-wiles-departure-maha/">postelection episode</a> of Joe Rogan’s podcast, Calley Means, a former senior adviser to Kennedy, accused senior White House officials of allowing corporate interests to undermine MAHA’s goals. Dissatisfaction also spilled over to MAHA supporters in the general public, with one <a href="https://www.kff.org/public-opinion/health-care-in-the-2026-midterm-election/?entry=table-of-contents-the-role-of-maha">postelection poll</a> finding that just over half of MAHA supporters feel the Trump administration made Americans’ health and well-being better throughout his second term in office.</p>

<p>Dissatisfaction with Trump, however, tells only part of the story. Another KFF poll conducted just before the election found that 42% of MAHA-supporting voters considered <a href="https://www.kff.org/public-opinion/health-care-in-the-2026-midterm-election/?entry=table-of-contents-the-role-of-maha">lowering healthcare costs</a> their top health priority. By comparison, 21% prioritized restricting food additives, and 10% chose vaccine safety. Among voters more broadly, 55% believed Trump’s policies increased their healthcare costs, and 83% of those voters reported voting for Democrats. Most MAHA supporters, however, <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/exit-polls">continued to vote for Republicans</a>. </p>

<p>Supporting a movement, embracing its policy priorities and casting a ballot for its candidates do not necessarily go hand in hand. Americans can support MAHA’s goals without identifying with the movement or voting for its candidates. Likewise, MAHA supporters may vote Republican even when they are dissatisfied with Trump’s health policies. MAHA’s electoral losses, therefore, tell us little about how much support its ideas enjoy.</p>

            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771654/original/file-20261112-64-ydbkyx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Vice President JD Vance, right, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., wave while standing in front of a blue backdrop that says MAHA Summit" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771654/original/file-20261112-64-ydbkyx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771654/original/file-20261112-64-ydbkyx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771654/original/file-20261112-64-ydbkyx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771654/original/file-20261112-64-ydbkyx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771654/original/file-20261112-64-ydbkyx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771654/original/file-20261112-64-ydbkyx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771654/original/file-20261112-64-ydbkyx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">MAHA’s agenda continues to hold sway in the Trump administration.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Vance/37d9821ae55f424ab9252f00a5e6b2d3/photo">AP Photo/Rod Lamkey, Jr.</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>MAHA remains the status quo in Washington</h2>

<p>Despite its electoral losses, MAHA still holds considerable influence in Washington. Kennedy still leads HHS, where he can continue reshaping how the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention <a href="https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/kennedy-rewrites-rules-membership-us-vaccine-advisory-panel-2026-04-06/">steers vaccine recommendations</a> in a direction that aligns with his vaccine-skeptical views. These efforts face growing scrutiny amid <a href="https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/childhood-vaccines/most-americans-confused-about-rfk-jr-s-stance-measles-vaccine-views-dim-his">public confusion over Kennedy’s vaccine guidance</a> and reports that he sought to <a href="https://theconversation.com/cdc-vs-pennsylvania-why-conflicting-public-health-messages-jeopardize-public-safety-291239">remove measles-related deaths from CDC statistics</a>. </p>

<p>Kennedy appears undeterred by MAHA’s electoral setbacks. Following the election, he <a href="https://x.com/SecKennedy/status/2118808625510813795">praised incoming White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller</a>, declaring, “Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken.” </p>

<p>MAHA’s continued influence in the Trump administration, however, will face new obstacles now that Democrats control Congress. Facing greater opposition, the administration may increasingly rely on executive actions, including <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/08/delivering-gold-standard-childhood-vaccine-recommendations-for-americans/">executive orders</a>, <a href="https://www.statnews.com/2026/10/26/health-data-interoperability-hti5-relaxes-privacy-security-requirements/">new</a> <a href="https://news.bloomberglaw.com/health-law-and-business/gender-dysphoria-dropped-as-disability-under-trump-hhs-rule">federal regulations</a> and <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/MAHA-Report-The-White-House.pdf">agency</a> <a href="https://www.npr.org/sections/shots-health-news/2025/04/16/nx-s1-5366676/autism-cdc-rates-rfk-research">reports</a>, to advance its health policies. However, Congress can also investigate HHS decisions and use its control over federal spending to limit what the agency can do.</p>

<h2>What’s next for MAHA?</h2>

<p>MAHA’s political future remains uncertain. Some supporters may gradually move toward Democrats, particularly those concerned about corporate influence, pharmaceutical industry accountability and food safety. These concerns <a href="https://www.kff.org/health-costs/public-opinion-on-prescription-drugs-and-their-prices/#caa040a6-6e54-4977-9b45-f0d168f535eb">cross partisan lines</a>, giving Democrats an opportunity to appeal to voters dissatisfied with Trump but still supportive of MAHA’s priorities.</p>

<p>MAHA could also become a movement independent of Trump and MAGA. It could bring together Americans who care about health and wellness, distrust major institutions and oppose corporate influence over food and medicine. Kennedy’s independent presidential campaign <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/08/23/as-rfk-jr-exits-a-look-at-who-supported-him-in-the-2024-presidential-race/">attracted as much as 15% support among voters</a> in July 2024. This showed that an alternative to the two major parties could attract substantial support.</p>

<p>Whether MAHA remains tied to Trump’s increasingly divided coalition will shape its future beyond his presidency. The frustrations and health concerns that fueled its rise among Americans have not disappeared.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296093/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

One prime example: In a postelection episode of Joe Rogan’s podcast, Calley Means, a former senior adviser to Kennedy, accused senior White House officials of allowing corporate interests to undermine MAHA’s goals

Dissatisfaction also spilled over to MAHA supporters in the general public, with one postelection poll finding that just over half of MAHA supporters feel the Trump administration made Americans’ health and well-being better throughout his second term in office
Dissatisfaction with Trump, however, tells only part of the story
Another KFF poll conducted just before the election found that 42% of MAHA-supporting voters considered lowering healthcare costs their top health priority
By comparison, 21% prioritized restricting food additives, and 10% chose vaccine safety
Among voters more broadly, 55% believed Trump’s policies increased their healthcare costs, and 83% of those voters reported voting for Democrats
Most MAHA supporters, however, continued to vote for Republicans
Supporting a movement, embracing its policy priorities and casting a ballot for its candidates do not necessarily go hand in hand
Americans can support MAHA’s goals without identifying with the movement or voting for its candidates
Likewise, MAHA supporters may vote Republican even when they are dissatisfied with Trump’s health policies
MAHA’s electoral losses, therefore, tell us little about how much support its ideas enjoy
MAHA’s agenda continues to hold sway in the Trump administration
MAHA remains the status quo in Washington Despite its electoral losses, MAHA still holds considerable influence in Washington
Kennedy still leads HHS, where he can continue reshaping how the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention steers vaccine recommendations in a direction that aligns with his vaccine-skeptical views
These efforts face growing scrutiny amid public confusion over Kennedy’s vaccine guidance and reports that he sought to remove measles-related deaths from CDC statistics
Kennedy appears undeterred by MAHA’s electoral setbacks
Following the election, he praised incoming White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller , declaring, “Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration
It’s time to unleash the Kraken.” MAHA’s continued influence in the Trump administration, however, will face new obstacles now that Democrats control Congress

<title>Republican gerrymandering worked pretty well in Texas and Florida, even if it backfired in North Carolina and Ohio</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771383/original/file-20261111-64-q1watl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3217%2C2144&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Gerrymandering in advance of the 2026 midterms did not always produce the intended effect.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/midterm-election-royalty-free-image/2263696390?phrase=gerrymandering&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Douglas Rissing, iStock/Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>During the 2026 election cycle, <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/redistricting-and-census/changing-the-maps-tracking-mid-decade-redistricting">Republicans enacted a series of gerrymanders</a> – a form of partisan redistricting – in a handful of states to give them a disproportionate edge over Democrats in their congressional delegations. Democrats responded with a <a href="https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/02/supreme-court-allows-california-to-use-congressional-map-benefitting-democrats/">successful redistricting effort in California</a> and an <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/05/08/nx-s1-5805193/redistricting-virginia-trump-midterms">unsuccessful one in Virginia</a>.</p>

<p>Gerrymandering has obvious implications for fairness and democracy, characterized by some as politicians picking their voters, not voters picking their politicians.</p>

<p>There’s also a practical consideration for those doing the gerrymandering: The efforts can fail when they overplay their hand. </p>

<p>By spreading their supportive voters across many districts, parties can create more seats that may lean in their direction. But if spread too thin, <a href="https://theconversation.com/3-reasons-republicans-redistricting-power-grab-might-backfire-262553">these efforts can backfire</a> and net seats for the other party, particularly in a “wave” election year that favors the other party. This unintended consequence is <a href="https://sites.socsci.uci.edu/%7Ebgrofman/140%20Grofman%20and%20Brunell.%20%202005%20%20The%20Art%20of%20the%20Dummymander....pdf">often referred to as a “dummymander</a>.”</p>

<p>So, with such massive Democratic majorities poised to enter the 120th Congress, did Republican attempts to gerrymander actually end up costing them some seats in the U.S. House? </p>

<p>The answer isn’t as clear-cut as you might think.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771599/original/file-20261112-64-1mzryt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large group of people posing for a photo on massive stone steps in front of a building with pillars." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771599/original/file-20261112-64-1mzryt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771599/original/file-20261112-64-1mzryt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771599/original/file-20261112-64-1mzryt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771599/original/file-20261112-64-1mzryt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771599/original/file-20261112-64-1mzryt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771599/original/file-20261112-64-1mzryt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771599/original/file-20261112-64-1mzryt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Dummymanders in North Carolina and Ohio?</h2>

<p>Republican state legislatures in Ohio and North Carolina <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/redistricting-and-census/changing-the-maps-tracking-mid-decade-redistricting">redrew their congressional maps in 2025</a>, crafting a set of districts they believed would maximize the number of seats they could win in the House. </p>

<p>Despite both states being traditionally competitive in statewide elections, their state legislatures drew a collection of seats Republicans believed they would win: 12 of these 15 new seats in Ohio and 11 out of 14 in North Carolina included a majority of voters who voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election.</p>



<p>But in 2026, Democrats across the country <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/house-districts-flipped-2026-midterm-elections/">won dozens of seats</a> that had previously seemed out of reach, including districts Trump won by double digits in 2024. Many of these seats were in heavily gerrymandered Republican seats.</p>

<p>In Ohio and North Carolina, the size and scope of the midterm backlash against Trump and his party put many of the seats Republicans targeted in these states, including ones Trump won by as many as 20 points, in serious jeopardy.  </p>

<p>In the end, the Democratic wave overcame so many Trump-won seats in these states that their new delegations to Congress may be more Democratic than they would have been without the gerrymanders.</p>

<h2>Democrats held the line in the deep South</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-6028588/redistricting-efforts-failed-republicans">Texas and Florida also targeted a series of Democrat-held seats</a> to flip their way in 2026. Nine such seats across these two states, as well as a vulnerable seat held by Democratic U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures in Alabama, were the targets of gerrymanders that created new districts that Trump won in 2024, all by 9 percentage points or more.</p>

<p>But once the 2026 Democratic wave swept through the deep South, these gerrymanders were essentially canceled out. Despite the gains the party projected, Republicans in these three states appear likely to enter the 120th Congress with delegations the same size as they had in the 119th.</p>

<p>Other Republican gerrymandering attempts were successful, but only barely. In Tennessee’s 9th District, the last remaining Democratic seat in the state <a href="https://sos.tn.gov/announcements/2026-congressional-redistricting">was gerrymandered</a> into a district Donald Trump won by 21 points in 2024. Republicans did <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/11/03/us/elections/results-tennessee-us-house-9.html">hold that seat</a> as expected, but only by 2,500 votes, or just over 1 percentage point.</p>

<h2>Gerrymanders that worked – and didn’t</h2>

<p>Many of these gerrymanders were not maximally successful. But were they true dummymanders?</p>

<p>In North Carolina and Ohio it does appear that Republicans overplayed their hand by counting on past Trump voters in a national environment that proved so favorable to the Democrats. </p>

<p>In Ohio, a gerrymander that aimed for a two-thirds Republican majority in their House delegation will net them <a href="https://www.wosu.org/politics-government/2026-11-04/ohio-democrats-overcome-congressional-gerrymandering-likely-flipping-three-seats">less than half of that in the 120th Congress</a>. That outcome ended up producing a more representative result, one that was roughly in line with the two parties’ 2026 popular vote shares in the state.</p>

<p>North Carolina was a more drastic dummymander: The Republicans aimed to design districts where they would win seats accounting for almost two-thirds of their congressional delegation. But the party is <a href="https://carolinapublicpress.org/82900/gop-gerrymander-backfires-in-nc-as-states-congressional-map-goes-blue/">currently poised to hold</a>, at best, less than one-third of their state’s seats.</p>

<p>And California, which Democrats gerrymandered in reaction to Republican efforts in other states, is <a href="https://calmatters.org/newsletter/california-midterm-gerrymander/">a partisan success story</a>. The state is projected to send only 8% of their delegation to the House as Republicans, despite voting 30% for Republicans statewide.</p>

<iframe title="Comparing Republican popular votes and congressional delegations in gerrymandered states" aria-label="Grouped column chart" id="datawrapper-chart-0btwS" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/0btwS/1/" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" style="border: none;" width="100%" height="597"></iframe>

<p>In Texas and Florida the story is more complicated. Democrats in those states retained most of the seats they held that their Republican legislatures targeted in their gerrymanders, thanks to <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/latino-voters-propel-democrats-to-big-wins-with-leftward-swing">historic shifts by Hispanic voters</a> who had voted for Trump in the 2024 election.</p>

<p>But gerrymanders can be effective beyond marginal, targeted districts. Taken as a whole, Texas’ and Florida’s district boundaries were drawn so favorably for Republicans that even a Democratic tsunami managed only to keep these states’ delegations identical in the next Congress, since many other districts remained safe for Republicans.</p>

<p>In these states, Republicans still enjoy a greater proportion of House seats than their popular vote margins would reflect. And in a less Democrat-leaning election cycle, many of these gerrymandered seats could very well shift back toward Republicans.</p>

<h2>Failed GOP gerrymanders would have produced an even bigger blue wave</h2>

<p>As poor as the outcome of the 2026 midterms was for Republicans, it could have been even worse. In fact, some Republican states might count themselves lucky that their attempts to gerrymander failed in the lead-up to the midterms.</p>

<p>In traditionally Republican states such as <a href="https://statecourtreport.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/chaos-missouris-redistricting-litigation">Missouri</a> and <a href="https://redistricting.lls.edu/case/lwv-of-utah-v-utah-state-legislature/">Utah</a>, courts struck down gerrymanders that would have created a series of districts that <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Missouri_ahead_of_the_2026_elections">Trump won</a> by around <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Utah_ahead_of_the_2026_elections">20 percentage points</a>. If the gerrymanders had not been struck down, Democrats’ shocking success in similar districts across the country could have netted them as many as five additional seats in these states.</p>

<p>A similar situation played out in <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/indiana-redistricting-vote-fails-senate-trump/">Indiana</a> and <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/05/26/nx-s1-5831996/redistricting-midterms-trump-south-carolina">South Carolina</a>. New maps pushed by Trump that failed in their state legislatures were intended to produce even more lopsided Republican gains. But <a href="https://www.cookpolitical.com/analysis/house/house-overview/could-blue-wave-drown-out-mid-decade-redistricting">analysis from the Cook Political Report</a> found that these maps might have netted Democrats as many as six out of South Carolina’s seven House seats, and eight out of Indiana’s nine. Instead, Democrats seem likely to end up with only a pair of seats in each state.</p>

<h2>What’s next in gerrymandering wars?</h2>

<p>The 2026 election cycle demonstrates that gerrymandering is a far more complex and dynamic proposition than it is often treated by pundits and parties. </p>

<p>Wave elections of this size can often overcome the intended effects of gerrymandered maps, but subsequent elections might find them much more effective. Plus, parties often draw gerrymandered maps based on the previous election’s presidential results – a measure that may be less reliable as voters continue to make more unexpected choices.</p>

<p>Moreover, both red and blue states are dealing with the aftermath of the <a href="https://constitutioncenter.org/blog/the-supreme-courts-callais-decision-sets-new-framework-for-racial-gerrymandering">Louisiana v. Callais Supreme Court decision</a>, which made the gerrymandering of racial groups easier to do without court interventions. Over the next two years, Republicans may attempt to implement even more new maps in many new states, particularly in the South. Those new districts will likely aim to dilute <a href="https://www.hks.harvard.edu/faculty-research/policy-topics/fairness-justice/what-louisiana-v-callais-means-voting-rights-act">majority-Black districts</a> that are no longer protected by the Voting Rights Act.</p>

<p>Meanwhile, Democratic state governments <a href="https://www.thebulwark.com/p/democrat-not-backing-off-their-own-redistricting-push-after-2026-midterms">appear poised to continue</a> with their pushback against last cycle’s Republican efforts with gerrymanders of their own over the next two years.</p>

<p>But the Republican redistricting failures of the 2026 cycle, including their near misses, should make both parties cautious about future attempts.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295944/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
