title: Do the Dems need new leadership?
excerpt: Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill in June 2026. | Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in  Tod
body: Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill in June 2026. | Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

Hi readers, happy Friday! Today, we’re saying farewell — for now — to “Democrats in array.” Not quite two weeks after winning the 2026 midterms by a historic margin , the party has a leadership fight on its hands.  On Thursday evening, Sen

Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, made it official: He’s challenging current Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer for the title of majority leader next year, promising a bolder and more aggressive agenda for the party.  “It is about answering the call of the American people,” Van Hollen told MS NOW host Jen Psaki when he announced his candidacy on her show. “The call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual

And to do that, I think we need new leadership.” Newly elected Democrats Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) and Peggy Flanagan (D-MN), each of whom defeated more leadership-aligned Democrats in their Senate primaries, are backing his bid
But Van Hollen will have an uphill climb to win the job, which is set to be decided in a closed-door vote early next month
Schumer, 75, has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, starting in 2017, and says he’s confident he will have the votes to be reelected in December
Searching for “fighters” The Senate is the only chamber currently dealing with an active leadership fight, but it’s not the only one with some leadership angst
In the House, current Democratic minority leader Hakeem Jeffries is the overwhelming favorite to become the new speaker in January (he currently lacks any Democratic challengers)

But not everyone is happy about it, as my colleague Astead Herndon reported on Thursday .  The divide, he argues — both in the Schumer-Van Hollen showdown and frustrations with Jeffries — is not really about progressive versus moderate

Instead, he says, it’s about an energized, angry Democratic base looking for fighters to lead the party into what’s almost certain to be a combative final two years of the Trump administration, and a sense that neither Schumer nor Jeffries are ready to meet the moment.  It’s not just a problem for this cycle, either: Democrats won so widely last week that they’re very likely to hang onto their majorities at least through the 2028 election,  Eric Levitz points out .  There’s nothing to say that Democrats will have the same leaders in two years (particularly Schumer, who’s up for reelection in 2028 but may either retire or face a serious primary challenge).  But the intra-party debate that we’re watching play out right now is effectively a preview of the higher-stakes fight to come in 2028, when Democrats could also have control of the presidency — and their freest legislative hand since the 2008 election.  As Eric writes , that will come with some real challenges, not least that Democrats currently appear to be facing an impossible trio of economic promises, one of which they’ll likely need to break
But it will also be a moment of opportunity — if the party’s leaders are ready for it

title: Why the left and right are both cheering Jensen Huang’s downfall

body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the Nvidia/Japan AI Ecosystem Reception in Tokyo on July 16, 2026. | Philip Fong/AFP via Getty Images Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden downfall is in a sense shocking, considering his wealth, global fame, and role leading what was until recently the world’s most valuable company

But Huang’s immense influence in Washington — and particularly in President Donald Trump’s Washington — has long been intensely controversial among a surprisingly diverse cross-section of the political, business, and tech advocacy world
And his ouster not only drives a wedge through Trump’s second-term coalition, it could usher in a major change in how the US steers the AI revolution

Huang — who resigned this week after allegations he’d had affairs with two Nvidia employees and one Chinese businesswoman who some US officials claim was spying on him for the Chinese government — has been crucial in helping shape the Trump administration’s AI policies
That’s perhaps no surprise, given that Nvidia’s advanced chips are crucial to the AI revolution
His many critics, however, say Huang’s influence has been deeply harmful

Their main objection? They believe the Trump administration hasn’t been doing enough to stop China from getting or accessing advanced AI chips — in part because of Huang’s lobbying and sway with the president
This coalition of Huang critics spans the political spectrum
It includes right-wing China hawks and the bipartisan foreign policy establishment , who want to win an AI race against China
It includes economic populists in both parties, who resent China’s economic sway
It even includes some leading members of the Trump administration itself — Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have reportedly pushed for tighter chip restrictions
It also contains some even odder bedfellows
The coalition includes people who want to slow down the AI race, like the tech safety advocates who warn that advanced AI could cause human extinction
Yet it also includes two major US frontier AI companies, OpenAI and Anthropic , who hope to impede the growth of Chinese competitors by limiting their access to chips
All of these disparate groups come together around the core idea that the US urgently needs to do more to stop advanced chips from getting to China
Selling AI chips to China is like “selling nuclear weapons to North Korea,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said
Standing against them all — and often getting his way with Trump — has been Jensen Huang

Beyond the obvious — Nvidia’s business is selling chips, and Huang wants to be able to sell more chips in more places — Huang is associated with a camp in the AI policy debate that some have dubbed with “let it rip.” Along with former White House AI czar David Sacks , Huang has scoffed at warnings that AI could cause human extinction, calling them “irresponsible” and “doomsday narratives.” He’s also dismissed some national security concerns, saying that being a “China hawk” was a “badge of shame” and said that the bigger risk to American influence over AI would be US companies losing market share around the world

So Huang’s ouster and the claims of Chinese espionage around it have opened up an opportunity for a shakeup in US policy — and a rare chance for those China hawks to potentially investigate, undermine, and push out their rivals, while seizing the policy reins around chip exports.  Trump administration officials who want tougher restrictions have their knives out for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a frequent ally of Huang’s
There’s a bipartisan push in Congress for new export controls legislation before the end of the year
Congressional Republican committee chairs are demanding Huang and Lutnick come in and testify in the coming weeks , before Democrats take over Congress
Plus, there are the partisan incentives for Democrats to dig into the question of what Trump knew about all this (he was reportedly briefed on the spy concerns last fall )

And there are political incentives for ambitious Republicans to find an issue on which they can distance themselves from an unpopular administration without antagonizing their conservative base.  With so many different forces invested in the outcome, you can bet this topic will continue to dominate headlines for months to come — with unpredictable results for both the new Democratic Congress, the future of the GOP, and the AI boom

The many critics of Jensen Huang’s influence on the Trump administration In Washington itself, the most influential faction opposed to Huang is the bipartisan national security establishment, most of whom strongly believe in the necessity of competing with China for global influence.  These “ China hawks ” were influential in the Biden administration and have historically been dominant in GOP administrations and on GOP-controlled congressional committees

And many of them have been flabbergasted at Trump’s policies toward China and Chips this term. “I don’t think we should be using any American technology to uplift China’s capabilities in AI given how era-defining this technology will be in national security and in our economy,” Vivek Chilukuri of the Center for a New American Security, a center-left think tank, told me. “A company’s going to argue for this, that’s what companies do
But the interest of any one company should not be trumping the national security of the United States
Moving further right, there’s a MAGA-aligned faction that is skeptical of foreign wars such as Trump’s conflict in Iran — but even some of them are still quite antagonistic to China
Take, for instance, Trump’s onetime campaign manager and White House adviser Steve Bannon

He’s been furiously protesting Huang’s influence on the administration for more than a year — in September 2025, he argued that Huang should be arrested for being “an agent of influence of the Chinese Communist Party,” and argued we needed to “shut down” China’s “access to technology, chips, and training.” Advocates and politicians focused on economic issues and reining in corporate power also have long criticized Nvidia

Oren Cass of the center-right group American Compass wrote an article titled “Break up Nvidia” last year, arguing that “its excessive concentration of power is exactly what antitrust law intends to combat.”  Meanwhile, the left, Sen
Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), a longtime critic of Big Tech, has frequently suggested Huang was corruptly influencing the Trump administration

At a hearing in June, she mentioned that Huang or his company had donated to Trump’s inauguration and his White House ballroom project. “If it’s not plain old-fashioned bribery, it sure smells like it,” she said
Many in the AI safety advocacy world have also long criticized — and feared — Nvidia
That’s in part because they hope slowing down sales of AI chips abroad could slow what they view as a dangerous race to superintelligence

Additionally, after AI safety fears hit the mainstream in September due to Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s resignation and viral warnings, Huang took an increasingly public role in dismissing such fears

Other AI safety advocates cite the company as having a chilling effect on public debate. “For months now, I’ve heard about widespread fear among think tank researchers and policy experts who publish work against Nvidia’s interests,” AI safety researcher Steven Adler wrote last year . “If you speak with people in-the-know at AI companies, fear of retaliation from Nvidia is a major concern when staking out policy positions.” Indeed, OpenAI and Anthropic are highly dependent on Nvidia for its chips, so open criticism of the company is not common

Yet those big two US AI labs have been at odds with Nvidia in urging the Trump administration to do more to crack down on Chinese access to advanced chips, and to more heavily scrutinize Chinese “open source” AI models
But to Huang and others in his camp, the growth of Chinese AI is a feature, not a bug

Sacks, for instance, has repeatedly argued that “open weight” or “open source” models — which make their parameters publicly available, in contrast to the proprietary models of OpenAI and Anthropic — would help avert “an unsafe and dystopian future where advanced AI capabilities are centralized and controlled by only a few hands.” The leading open weight models are currently from Chinese companies

Huang has also used a more straightforward argument: that what’s good for Nvidia is good for the United States of America. “American technology has to win across the world at every single layer,” he said in May . “If we can export chips, we should.” Now it will be left to Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, to carry that message, instead of a rock-star founder with a global cult following that’s drawn comparisons to Steve Jobs at his peak at Apple

title: OpenAI is betting a data center rebrand will make you hate them less
excerpt: An under-construction data center in Saline, Michigan, on October 6, 2026. | Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Republicans weren’t the only b
body: An under-construction data center in Saline, Michigan, on October 6, 2026. | Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Republicans weren’t the only big losers in last week’s midterms: Across the country, voters also backed restrictions on data centers and elected candidates promising tougher oversight of AI companies

Out of 41 local ballot initiatives limiting the data center buildout, 40 of them passed, according to the New York Times .  The AI industry knows it was a tough cycle: Chris Lehane, the chief global affairs officer for OpenAI, told Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram that “I could take my shirt off and show you my [metaphorical] bruises if you want.” Now, OpenAI is figuring out how to move forward
Lehane talked with Sean from rural Texas, where he said he was on a “listening and learning” tour of communities around the site of a massive OpenAI data center

They discussed the lessons of the midterm election, why OpenAI would prefer that we call data centers “compute campuses,” and why Lehane thinks the 2028 presidential election will largely revolve around AI — just not in the same way that 2026 did. “I just don’t think it’s going to be good enough for a candidate from either party to emerge from their primary by simply being the person who’s against things,” Lehane said
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify

You guys at OpenAI, in the wake of this shellacking, put out this big document saying that you’re going to be listening, you’re going to be learning, you’re going to be empowering local people and bringing jobs

You’re also, in this document, rebranding data centers to “compute campuses,” which when I say it, I have trouble not laughing because it sounds like a bit of a joke to meet everyone’s concerns with a rebrand
Please tell us why you think this could work or why it’s a good idea
We were very intentional in actually using that phrase
And we did it with the full knowledge that people would potentially be skeptical of it
But I do think there’s an intent behind provoking this conversation.  Data centers have existed for 20-odd years and at some level they’re the proverbial empty box in a pasture
And they’re called data centers because that’s in fact what they were
When people talked about the cloud, this is actually where the cloud was housed, where you would load data if you were streaming a video, if you were ordering something from a delivery service
These AI facilities are really fundamentally different
What is being generated at these facilities is something called compute

And compute is just the raw computing power that it takes to train AI systems and then run AI tools and products when you’re using them.  Second of all, they’re different because [of] the amount of jobs that do get created directly
This is not half a dozen people in that empty box
These are real jobs, these are six-figure jobs
They are also huge opportunities for economic transformation if a community approaches it in a really strategic way and companies like ours do our part to work with those communities
We’re not just building in the communities, we’re building with the communities
You’re out there in Texas because essentially, data centers and artificial intelligence have a PR problem

Seventy percent of the country, maybe more than that, says that they’re against data centers, or “compute campuses,” as you’re now calling them.  Why do you think it is that data centers have such a public relations issue in this country right now? There’s a variety of factors, but before even jumping into those, I do think it’s worth noting and worth emphasizing that we have roughly six of these projects up and running in the country
They’re in different stages of being built out and developed, but each and every one of them is moving forward
I do think that there is a right way to build these and perhaps a wrong way and we can get into that

Do you think that you guys were doing it the wrong way before? This goes to why I think we’ve actually been able to get approvals for each of the projects that we are doing.  I think each of the individual projects themselves have been some version of a laboratory of democracy, where you actually learn from each project and apply those learnings to the next project

But I do think we got the fundamental insight right at the beginning, which is to actually go on the ground, listen, learn, hold yourself accountable and take the feedback and build your facility with the community

I think that for a lot of communities, folks were coming in, they were building data centers, they were then transferring the electricity costs to the public, they were potentially impacting their water, they weren’t necessarily doing the type of community investments that you should do if you’re going to be building with a community.  Where we’ve really tried to differ ourselves — and again, we’re not perfect, we’re learning every step of the way — but I do think that we have successfully applied the baseline as we’ve gone through this, which is, we make sure we’re paying for our own electricity, our own energy
Point two is that we make sure we’re preserving water
We have something called closed water loops
I know this is getting a little bit technical, but think of these as sort of large radiators
You fill it up once and therefore you’re able to preserve the water
One thing that seems clear from the election results is that there’s just not a lot of trust

Now there’s going to be a new Congress, and various components of said Congress are pledging to do more to regulate AI and tech.  It wasn’t so long ago that the head of your company, Sam Altman, was calling for Congress to get more involved
Does that call still stand now that it’s a different Congress that might be more inclined to come down hard on AI? When it comes to data centers, these are typically state or local issues

We envisioned that as state legislation that would actually make these requirements for folks who are building data centers to help give the public confidence that there’s going to be a real material benefit for them
I think what you’re referring to was our call as OpenAI for there to be national-level mandatory safety requirements for the frontier labs who are building AI
We thought about that and called for it before the election

We think it’s more important than ever.  Back in early September, I had a blog post out there that talked about this idea that the policy window was opening up to create a real opportunity to pass those mandatory safety requirements
And the reason I talked about the policy window being opened up is that you could clearly see where the politics were going, what was likely to happen with the election.  You’re in Washington, DC

title: Democrats made shocking gains with religious voters — but not everywhere
excerpt: Voters arrive to cast their ballots at a polling location inside St
body: Voters arrive to cast their ballots at a polling location inside St

Patrick Parish Center in White Lake, Michigan on Election Day. | Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images One of the most eye-opening aspects of last week’s midterms was the new cohort of religious politicians it sent to Congress — many of them part of a wave of Democratic-leaning Christians
Another striking feature was the dramatic shift among many religious voters
For years, American politics has seemed stuck on a partisan track, with religious-identified voters shifting more firmly to the right, and the nonreligious tacking to the left
There are a few exceptions , of course — Jewish voters, Latino Catholics, and Black Protestants, who have stayed firmly Democratic — but the broader tide has flowed clearly one way
Key takeaways This year’s blue tsunami carried voters everywhere to the left; it also scrambled voting trends in America’s religious electorate
Catholics shifted hard to the left after Donald Trump won their vote by a double-digit margin in 2024
Jewish voters were still strongly Democratic, though there are clear signs of lower support than in previous electoral cycles
Other religious groups, mainline Protestants and Muslims, contributed to a diverse Democratic coalition — while evangelicals appeared less enthusiastic to turn out
The 2026 vote, for the first time in a while, makes that picture look less certain
Based on exit polls, county-level data, and some post-election analysis, we already have a handful of intriguing signs of change

The data is still early and patchy, but it appears that Catholic voters around the country moved left, evangelical Christians stayed home, and some Jewish voters dug in against the anti-Israel rhetoric and moved rightward
And in Utah, generational differences, particularly among Mormons, may be starting to change the political makeup of a rock-ribbed conservative state
There are caveats: Wave elections, especially when they’re of the historic proportions of last week’s Democratic tsunami, can obscure and cloud these changes
When everyone moves in one direction, it can be hard to distinguish specific storylines

And with religion, as with any single voter attribute, it can be difficult to tease out just how much faith and religious identity influenced vote choice, as opposed to working in combination with race, class, and concerns about issues like affordability and immigration
And better data is still to come; the gold standard of voter roll-validated studies , like the Pew Research Center’s , won’t be available until next year

Yet that combination of factors also suggests a new possibility for our politics: that religious voters of all creeds can come to function as swing voters too, cracking up old alliances, like on the religious right , and offering the hint of new winning coalitions, as Catholics and mainline Protestant Christians seem to have done for the Democrats
The largest shift: Catholic voters swung against the GOP Catholics play a special role in American politics
They spent much of the last century operating as a solid Democratic bloc , reaching a peak in the 1960s when John F
Kennedy, the first Catholic president, won about 80 percent of their vote

Since then, they’ve gradually become more Republican, due to assimilation of former European Catholic immigrants, the rise of conservative activism over abortion and social issues, and the rise of the religious right
In the last two decades, Catholics have tended to reflect the views of the median American voter, evenly split in the 2012, 2016, and 2020 presidential elections
Across different polls and surveys, Catholics shifted decisively to the right: backing Trump 59-39 according to exit polls, and 55-43 , according to the Pew Research Center

Now, in a year in which Trump and Republicans frequently clashed with Pope Leo XIV and his bishops — over the Iran war, mass deportations, and immigration policy — Catholic voters again turned into a wild card
This year, according to exit polls , they swung left , with the margin shifting by more than 20 points
Democrats narrowly won the Catholic vote this time, 50-49
As a subgroup, that put Catholics up there with Asian voters, Latinos, urban and suburban voters, Gen Z and millennials as being the top groups that swung to the left this year

View Link Other estimates from the religion and politics scholar Ryan Burge show particularly noticeable shifts among white Catholics, swinging about 9 points toward Democrats, even if a majority of them still voted for Republican congressional candidates
In Texas, his analysis showed that counties with higher shares of Latino Catholics were much more likely to support the winning Democratic Senate candidate, James Talarico
The results were even more dramatic in the most Catholic House districts
Of the 12 districts with the highest share of Catholics, the average swing in the vote was about 15 points, and Democrats won eight of these seats, while gaining in all 12
Catholics have tended to basically operate like the median voter — swinging in the same direction as the overall popular vote

That makes it harder to pinpoint any unique motivators that caused Catholics to move against the GOP: Trump’s fights with Catholic leaders, the lack of a mobilized anti-abortion movement this year, or the affordability concerns that moved all voters
One notable exception here are Latino Catholics, who tend to be the most Democratic of the Catholic electorate, and most opposed to Trump’s immigration and deportation policies this cycle

It’s no coincidence that they’re concentrated in the Southwest, including those parts of Texas that swung toward Talarico and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa over both economic stress and anger over immigration enforcement
Does this all suggest the rise of a new Catholic swing vote? Potentially — combined with the decline in abortion politics in the US, and a more active Vatican

For the first time, the Church has an American pope, one who isn’t afraid to get involved with current affairs and push harder on Catholic social teachings (which align more with the Democratic Party’s views of society and the economy)
That could have meaningful repercussions heading into 2028

Though still very blue, some Jewish voters broke with the Democrats Jewish Americans, though they only make up about 2 percent of the American population, became a huge focus of political attention this year — in large part because of how central they are to Democratic coalitions (along with Black Americans, they are some of the most loyal Democratic voters), and because Israel became a flashpoint in American politics.  As Democrats made a dramatic shift in the last two years in how they talk about Israel and AIPAC, with increasingly open criticism of the Israeli government’s actions , some Jewish Democrats and Republicans responded with charges of antisemitism — and some Republicans started leaning into overt Islamophobia , particularly in Michigan

title: Why online gamblers are obsessed with table tennis
excerpt: If you were living in Colorado in May and bet on sports online, you’d statistically have been most likely to bet on professional basketball
body: If you were living in Colorado in May and bet on sports online, you’d statistically have been most likely to bet on professional basketball
The third-most wagered sport? Table tennis.  Colorado is almost certainly not an outlier
Table tennis occupies a similarly high ranking in Oregon , the only other state to provide sport-by-sport breakdowns of gambling revenue
And it’s likely true in every other state that allows sports gambling
This is a strange fact, one that’s been reported by a few local and national outlets

And beyond the bets involved, it’s also a window into where sports gambling is going, and how sports betting is morphing into something stranger and more destructive than dropping $100 on the New York Yankees to cover the spread on Saturday
There’s the old quip that the Holy Roman Empire was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire
In some sense, this is sports betting that involves neither sports nor betting
The gambling on table tennis isn’t really on the game of table tennis
It’s on a strange simulacrum of table tennis created solely for the purpose of creating more ways to gamble on it
For many of the people involved, it’s a kind of mindless, by-the-second slot machine rather than an informed wager on a player they might think can win
Ping-pong, in other words, has been reengineered into an addictive technology

The story of how table tennis came to occupy this outsized role in sports betting — and what it really looks like now — offers an unsettling peek at how fast all of this is moving, and how much the business of gambling can distort the real world around it

When most professional sports leagues shut down during the early stages of the Covid-19 pandemic, low-level, peculiar table tennis leagues in Eastern Europe popped up and were often the only game in town when it came to being able to place bets on sports

In May 2020 in Colorado, $6.5 million was wagered on table tennis, more than 25 percent of the statewide total — making it the most popular sport to bet on, simply because it was available.  But even after other sports came back, table tennis stuck around
In Colorado this past May, with every other sport back and operating, table tennis was bringing in $33.9 million, five times what it had been
The same pattern held in Oregon: In May 2020, table tennis was the most bet sport in Oregon , with $3.7 million wagered
By this past February , it was still the second-most bet sport, but now with $9.5 million wagered

LSports, a company that collects and provides the real-time data that sportsbooks use to take and pay out bets, has a report intended for gambling operators that provides some of the starkest information on this

Its advice: “Table tennis is no longer sports betting’s dark horse; it has become an essential asset for sportsbooks seeking 24/7 bettor engagement.” And a main reason for the appeal is the intense, constant flow of matches, so betting companies have “minimal gaps in their live offerings.” How is table tennis producing this much betting content? Sports aren’t on 24/7, and they have leagues, tournaments, offseasons, and training camps
The matches being bet on are not real leagues.  They have players that true fans of the sport would not recognize
They are played in strange, unmarked basements in Eastern Europe, with players whose names, if searched, reveal nothing beyond profiles on sports betting websites
The players’ abilities are clearly not at a professional level
Real, professional table tennis like World Table Tennis has packed arenas, high production value, professional announcers, and trophies for winners
Top athletes are elite physical specimens, able to hit small plastic balls 50 miles an hour at 150 rotations a second, with unfathomable hand-eye coordination

Players are national celebrities in their home countries.  When I logged on to DraftKings in Maryland and saw the “TT Elite” league available to bet on, the livestream of the match showed a single table in a bare, windowless, dark-gray room with no evident spectators, coaches, or even windows
It is the gambling tail wagging the sports dog; the sports exist solely to provide fodder to be bet on

How sports betting became an addictive product For those who don’t gamble on sports, there may still be a misunderstanding that what people are doing on DraftKings or FanDuel is dropping a basically simple bet or two a week, gambling on this or that team to cover the spread, or maybe betting a favorite player will win an end-of-season award

These apps, however, are now a labyrinth of parlays (combining multiple bets into one, all of which must win to pay out), prop bets (bets on some individual event, like a single point), and invitations to bet on the next quarter, the next point, the next five seconds

The betting dashboard gives an impression of nothing so much as a casino floor: overwhelming and constantly changing, giving the impression that skilled play is possible, whether or not that’s the case
Most of all, there are hundreds upon hundreds of ways to bet, a salami that can be sliced infinitely thin
This is very much how these companies intended it
Simple sports bets, like who will win a game, are actually not terribly profitable for bookmakers, who in fact can lose if betting lines are set incorrectly
This made companies actively seek to reengineer sports betting into slot machines, where bets come close to becoming totally abstracted button pushing

With prediction markets entering every nook and cranny of culture and politics, and casinos pushing states extraordinarily hard to get their products on our phones, it’s difficult to see where this stops. “Betting on ping-pong…is not a product built for recreation

It’s a product built to deliver constant action.”  Harry Levant, Public Health Advocacy Institute The Public Health Advocacy Institute (PHAI) filed a lawsuit against FanDuel, DraftKings, and the NFL , among others, for selling a “known addictive product.” The organization’s complaint filed on March 24 specifically notes of one of their client’s betting behavior that “if there were no U.S. games happening at a certain time, he would bet on international table tennis, again wagering repeatedly on every single point.” FanDuel did not respond to a request for comment on the allegations in the suit
DraftKings referred Vox to its trade group, the Sports Betting Alliance

I reached out to Harry Levant, PHAI’s director of gambling policy, and while he declined to expand on the facts in the complaint, he spoke generally about how someone might end up betting hundreds of times on table tennis a day. “By the time a person reaches pathological betting on ping-pong, they have often experienced many other forms of gambling, but more importantly, betting on ping-pong…is not a product built for recreation,” Levant said. “It’s a product built to deliver constant action.”  Joe Maloney, the president of the Sports Betting Alliance, a trade advocacy organization representing online sportsbooks, told me on the question of addictiveness that “the existence of any market doesn’t make it more or less addictive.” He went on to say that “the vast majority of people that enjoy these products, that walk into casinos, that download legal apps…overwhelmingly these are people that are able to enjoy these products responsibly, but there are some people that demonstrate problematic behavior, and those people need all the support.” One reason for the rise in table tennis betting is, frankly, its fakeness allows it to provide that action during otherwise barren hours

These are not prexisting and longstanding sports leagues that an interested consumer can decide they enjoy and place a bet on — they are ad hoc “leagues” created solely for the purpose of allowing sports betting for consumers at hours and during dates when more “normal” bets are not available, like PHAI’s client
So, availability is one reason for table tennis’s continued success on sportsbooks — the fact that one can find a bet at almost any time, any day of the year.  The second is the betting itself

title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
excerpt: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for i
body: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China

It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy
When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed

In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public
Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations
In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations
In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling
Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization

In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice

It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling
Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China
A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia

Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.  The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms
The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online
In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option
Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled
Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround

The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.   In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

title: Jensen Huang is out. What now?
excerpt: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in October 2026. | Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images The first big sex scandal of the AI era has taken down Jensen Huang , Nvidia’s co-fou
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in October 2026. | Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images The first big sex scandal of the AI era has taken down Jensen Huang , Nvidia’s co-founder and longtime CEO
Nvidia’s board of directors announced his resignation on Thursday morning and named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO

Huang has been making headlines all week after news broke Friday that he had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singaporean tech firm Megaspeed who the US government alleges was also a Chinese spy

The revelation Wednesday of a second extramarital affair , this time with an Nvidia employee reporting to Huang directly, added to the pressure, and another affair came to light later on Thursday after Huang’s ouster
The scandal has implications far beyond one company: Huang’s central role in the AI race can’t be overstated

It was his vision of an AI future that led him to pivot Nvidia from a small company making video game chips into the dominant player in making the chips that serve OpenAI , Anthropic, and Google’s computing needs
Huang is close friends with President Donald Trump’s and a leading voice in resisting efforts to slow AI progress
And he has pushed for the US to take a less hawkish position toward China’s own AI goals , a stance now called into question by his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy
Among its other impacts, the news has revived efforts on Capitol Hill to further restrict chip exports to China

To break down the national security implications of Huang’s departure, how the Trump administration is involved, and what it says about US AI industry writ large, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Garret De Vynck , a technology reporter at the Washington Post
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Nvidia has been called the central bank of AI, which is why it’s so important that we figure out what Jensen Huang may have disclosed to this alleged spy

How long has the president known about this, as far as we know? As far as we know, the president has known about the fact that Jensen Huang was in a relationship with someone that the US government thought was a spy for about a year
This circulated within the administration, and the decision was made not to tell Jensen
That doesn’t necessarily mean that it was automatically some kind of corrupt decision of President Trump protecting Jensen Huang
There’s all sorts of reasons why you might not want to tell someone they’re being spied on, the number one being that they might blow up the operation
Maybe you suspect that the person themselves knows that they’re being spied on and is willingly sharing information and you need some more time to gather that

It’s unclear why the US government specifically chose not to pull in Jensen Huang.  It’s also a little bit unclear whether he knows he was being spied on, or whether maybe he was told through some kind of back channel
He has said that he did not know that she was a spy and he is admitting to the affair, to the infidelity

He’s admitting to essentially breaking Nvidia’s code of conduct by sleeping with one of its customers, but he is not admitting at all to knowing that she was a spy and definitely not admitting to sharing any information willfully
It feels like this is the kind of thing that the government would investigate
There’s been reporting that the Commerce Department was involved with some kind of investigation, but that investigation came to an end and no one really knows why
The context here is that the United States and China are in an AI race

Going back to the first Trump administration, there’s been pretty aggressive export controls saying, “We don’t want China to get our tech so that they can develop AI.” And the Biden administration continued that
He increased the export controls on China
China was complaining very loudly about this
We want to win AI and we need to slow you guys down.’ When Trump came in, he actually lifted his foot off the gas a little bit
They didn’t throw the gates open and say, “You can have whatever you want
All American companies can sell whatever they want to China.” But he said, “Some AI chips that are less powerful than the state of the art

We can send those to Chinese companies.“ The other thing that national security experts have pointed out is that the Trump administration could theoretically have been doing more to stop the smuggling of computer chips to China
And that’s where this story gets so important for national security
Megaspeed is accused of essentially being a front for Chinese companies to get access to computer chips
Journalists have gone to Megaspeed’s office in Singapore where it’s based, and there were only a couple of people working there
It didn’t really seem like there was a lot going on

Nvidia has said all through this process over the last couple of years that, “No, we’ve checked it out, Megaspeed is a legitimate company and we’re not breaking the law when it comes to this.” There are a lot of questions and what everyone is focused on finding out, both journalists and I would say congressional Democrats when they come into office in the new year is, is there something more going on here? Is there something where the Chinese either convinced Jensen Huang to sell more chips to them or Jensen Huang himself, who has been advocating for selling more chips to China, essentially did this himself?  “I think there’s this real question of: Do we see a much stronger push to actually ramp up controls on China and how does Trump respond?” He’s been pressuring the president, he’s been donating to him , he’s been glad-handing with the president and the president has been listening more to this corporate executive who is his friend and who donated him a bunch of money rather than listening to China hawks or national security experts who say we should be limiting what China is able to access
That’s really where the locus of this investigation is going to be
It’s not so much that Jensen Huang had an affair

It’s more the fact that he himself is someone who has said we need to sell more computer chips to China and he was involved with an alleged Chinese spy, and he’s very close to the president and had influence on the president
Have they said anything? Are they going to call him in front of Congress for an investigation? Going forward, there are two big things here

title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
excerpt: A charged atmosphere in Antalya: COP31 is unfolding against a backdrop of war, spiking energy prices, and a world already blowing past the 1.5 °C warming thresh
body: A charged atmosphere in Antalya: COP31 is unfolding against a backdrop of war, spiking energy prices, and a world already blowing past the 1.5 °C warming threshold the Paris Agreement was designed to prevent
The money problem: Rich nations promised $300 billion a year by 2035 for climate action, but delivered less than half that in 2024

Fossil fuels back in the spotlight: After last year's final agreement didn't mention "fossil fuels" once, expect a fight over language—especially with cohosts Australia and Turkey both deeply tied to coal and gas. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148308" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey
COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world
Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20
This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis
And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular

Here’s what you should know about COP31.   In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked
This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US
President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change

That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.  Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels

In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.” So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming

There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.  Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.) The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas
The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage
The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country)
Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels
Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them
But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once

This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal
Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching

These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.   One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go
The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there
The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use
Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity
Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest
Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions

The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.  With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change
I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter
